title: Functions begin with a domain
subtitle: The domain is part of the mathematical object, not an afterthought.
definition: A set is a collection of distinct elements. Union means either set, intersection means both, and complement is relative to a specified universe. A function assigns exactly one output to each input in its domain $D$. Its range $f(D)$ is contained in its codomain $E$. A formula alone does not fix all of this data.
conditions: Every input in $D$ must have a unique image. For real formulas, exclude zero denominators, negative even-root arguments and nonpositive logarithm arguments.
proof: The vertical-line test follows directly from uniqueness: two points above one input would assign two outputs. A circle fails this test, while either semicircle becomes a function on an appropriate interval.
example: For $f(x)=\sqrt{x-1}/(x-2)$, the domain is $[1,2)\cup(2,\infty)$. The missing input $2$ remains excluded even if a later algebraic expression appears to allow it.
pitfall: Domain, codomain and range are different sets. A graph can leave some outputs unused.
task: Move the lower domain endpoint. Which part of the square-root graph is allowed?
insight: The domain is part of the mathematical object, not an afterthought.

title: Read a function’s shape
subtitle: Symmetry and monotonicity compress a graph into useful structural information.
definition: Piecewise functions use different rules on different subsets. Even functions reflect across the vertical axis; odd functions have half-turn symmetry about the origin. Strictly increasing means $x_1<x_2\Rightarrow f(x_1)<f(x_2)$. Polynomial, rational, power, trigonometric, exponential and logarithmic functions form the basic catalogue.
conditions: Even and odd symmetry require a domain symmetric about zero. Monotonicity is a statement on a specified interval.
proof: Substitute $-x$ and compare with $f(x)$ and $-f(x)$. To establish increasing behaviour directly, compare two arbitrary ordered inputs rather than a few plotted points.
example: $x^2$ is even and decreases on $(-\infty,0]$ but increases on $[0,\infty)$. The function $|x|$ is piecewise $-x$ for $x<0$ and $x$ for $x\ge0$.
pitfall: A function need not be even or odd. An isolated flat tangent does not rule out strict increase.
task: Shift the parabola horizontally. Does its original even symmetry survive?
insight: Symmetry and monotonicity compress a graph into useful structural information.

title: Transform and compose
subtitle: Follow the input through each operation in order.
definition: An outer transformation changes outputs; an inner transformation changes inputs. Addition, subtraction and products use the common domain; quotients further exclude zeros of the denominator. Composition means $(f\circ g)(x)=f(g(x))$.
conditions: For composition, require $x\in\operatorname{dom}g$ and $g(x)\in\operatorname{dom}f$. A nonzero inner scale $b$ changes horizontal lengths by $1/|b|$.
proof: If $(u,f(u))$ lies on the old graph, then $x=h+u/b$ gives the new point $(h+u/b,af(u)+k)$. This explains the reversed-looking horizontal scale.
example: With $f(x)=x^2$, $f(x-h)=(x-h)^2$ has vertex $(h,0)$. With $g(x)=\sqrt{x}$ and $f(x)=1/(x-1)$, the composition has domain $[0,\infty)\setminus\{1\}$.
pitfall: $f\circ g$ usually differs from $g\circ f$. Multiplying an input by two compresses the graph horizontally.
task: Move the shift and predict the vertex before observing it.
insight: Follow the input through each operation in order.

title: Approach a point
subtitle: Nearby behaviour and the value at the point answer different questions.
definition: A finite limit describes nearby outputs as the input approaches a point, excluding the point itself. Left and right limits restrict the direction of approach. Secant slopes and average velocities motivate limits as a way to extract instantaneous behaviour.
conditions: For the two-sided criterion, the domain has points approaching from both sides and both one-sided limits must equal the same finite number.
proof: If a two-sided limit exists, its estimate works on each side. Conversely, take the smaller of the left and right admissible distances to control both sides.
example: For $f(x)=(x^2-1)/(x-1)$ with $x\ne1$, cancellation gives $f(x)=x+1$, so the limit at $1$ is $2$ although $f(1)$ is undefined.
pitfall: A point value cannot determine a limit. Tables can suggest a limit but cannot establish behaviour at every sufficiently close input.
task: Bring the moving input towards the open circle. Compare the missing value with the limiting output.
insight: Nearby behaviour and the value at the point answer different questions.

title: Vertical asymptotes
subtitle: Unbounded behaviour must specify both direction and sign.
definition: An infinite limit states that outputs eventually exceed any prescribed height in magnitude, with the stated sign. A vertical asymptote occurs if at least one one-sided limit is infinite.
conditions: Infinity is not a real output. The sign and the side of approach matter; an unrestricted two-sided infinite limit needs agreement.
proof: Given $M>0$, choosing $\delta=1/M$ makes $0<x<\delta$ imply $1/x>M$. For $x<0$, the sign reverses.
example: $1/x$ tends to $+\infty$ from the right and $-\infty$ from the left. In contrast, $1/x^2$ tends to $+\infty$ from both sides.
pitfall: An undefined denominator does not by itself imply an asymptote: cancellation can produce a removable hole.
task: Move the positive cutoff towards zero and watch the reciprocal height.
insight: Unbounded behaviour must specify both direction and sign.

title: Limit laws and squeezing
subtitle: A uniform bound can settle a limit without following each oscillation.
definition: Finite limits respect sums, differences, products and constant multiples; quotients require a nonzero limiting denominator. The squeeze theorem traps an unknown function between two functions with the same limit. Cancelling a factor is legitimate on a punctured neighbourhood where that factor is nonzero.
conditions: For squeezing, the inequalities hold throughout a deleted neighbourhood. For real roots, keep the expression in its domain. Quotient laws do not evaluate an indeterminate form.
proof: Since $-1\le\sin(1/x)\le1$, multiplying the absolute-value inequality by $|x|$ gives the bound. Both $-|x|$ and $|x|$ tend to zero, so the trapped function does too.
example: $\lim_{x\to0}x\sin(1/x)=0$, despite infinitely rapid oscillation. The geometric sine inequality also gives $\lim_{x\to0}\sin x/x=1$ in radians.
pitfall: An oscillating factor need not converge for its product with a vanishing factor to converge.
task: Shrink the viewing neighbourhood. Watch the oscillation stay inside its envelope.
insight: A uniform bound can settle a limit without following each oscillation.

title: Make “close” precise
subtitle: One input neighbourhood must control every output in it.
definition: The challenger chooses an output tolerance $\varepsilon$. You must then choose one input tolerance $\delta$ that works for every admissible input. The order of the quantifiers is the substance of the definition.
conditions: $\delta$ may depend on $\varepsilon$ and the point, but not on the subsequently selected input. The implication must hold for all domain points in the deleted interval.
proof: For $f(x)=x^2$ at $a=1$, first impose $|x-1|<1$, so $|x+1|<3$. Then $|x^2-1|<3|x-1|$. Choose $\delta=\min(1,\varepsilon/3)$.
example: For the displayed $f(x)=2x$ at $a=1$, choosing $\delta=\varepsilon/2$ makes the horizontal input band map into the vertical output band around $L=2$.
pitfall: Finding a single nearby input inside the band is insufficient. You need control of the whole neighbourhood.
task: Change the output tolerance and compare it with the required input radius.
insight: One input neighbourhood must control every output in it.

title: Continuity and intermediate values
subtitle: Continuity prevents a graph from skipping intermediate output values.
definition: Continuity at a point means nearby outputs converge to the actual point value. Algebra and composition preserve continuity where defined. The intermediate value theorem says a continuous function on a closed interval takes every value between its endpoint values.
conditions: For IVT, $f$ is continuous on $[a,b]$ and the target lies between $f(a)$ and $f(b)$. Endpoints use one-sided continuity. A target strictly between endpoint values is reached in the interior.
proof: Bisect an interval whose endpoint values bracket the target. Retain a half that still brackets it. The shrinking intervals identify a point; continuity forces its function value to equal the target.
example: $f(x)=x^3-x$ on $[1,2]$ runs from $0$ to $6$, so every target in $(0,6)$ is attained. The plot varies that target and marks a corresponding point.
pitfall: IVT proves existence, not uniqueness. A jump can skip a target even when the endpoint values straddle it.
task: Choose a target height, then locate where the curve must cross it.
insight: Continuity prevents a graph from skipping intermediate output values.

title: From secants to a tangent
subtitle: The derivative extracts a stable rate from progressively smaller changes.
definition: The derivative is the finite limiting slope of secant lines. As a function of the base point it records local rates of change. In a position-time graph it is velocity; the derivative of velocity is acceleration.
conditions: The function must be defined near the base point and the two-sided difference quotient must have a finite limit. At domain endpoints use an explicitly one-sided notion.
proof: For $f(x)=x^2$, expansion gives $((a+h)^2-a^2)/h=2a+h$ when $h\ne0$. Taking the limit yields $f\prime(a)=2a$.
example: At $a=1$, the secant slope is $2+h$. Its limit is $2$, so the tangent line is $y=1+2(x-1)$.
pitfall: A secant slope for small $h$ is an approximation, not the definition’s completed limit.
task: Decrease the nonzero increment. Compare the secant with the fixed tangent.
insight: The derivative extracts a stable rate from progressively smaller changes.

title: Where differentiability fails
subtitle: A connected graph can still have no single tangent slope.
formula: f\text{ differentiable at }a\ \Rightarrow\ f\text{ continuous at }a
definition: Differentiability is stronger than continuity. Corners have disagreeing one-sided slopes; vertical tangents have unbounded slopes; discontinuities cannot be differentiable. Higher derivatives repeatedly differentiate the derivative function.
conditions: The implication uses a finite derivative. Existence of a second derivative requires the first derivative to exist nearby.
proof: Write $f(a+h)-f(a)=h\,[f(a+h)-f(a)]/h$. If the quotient tends to a finite derivative, the product tends to zero, proving continuity.
example: For $f(x)=|x|$, the right derivative at zero is $1$ and the left derivative is $-1$. The function is continuous there but has no derivative.
pitfall: Continuity does not guarantee differentiability. Nor must an existing derivative be continuous.
task: Approach the corner from each side and compare the two secant slopes.
insight: A connected graph can still have no single tangent slope.

title: Build derivatives from rules
subtitle: A changing product has one contribution from each changing factor.
definition: Constants differentiate to zero. The power rule, linearity, product and quotient rules assemble derivatives of algebraic functions. Trigonometric derivatives come from angle-addition formulas and the basic sine limit.
conditions: The functions are differentiable at the point; the quotient rule also requires $g\ne0$. Real-power rules are used only where the power is real and differentiable. Trigonometric angles are in radians.
proof: Add and subtract $f(x+h)g(x)$ inside the product difference. Divide by $h$ and pass to the limit, using differentiability to obtain continuity of the remaining factors.
example: For $f(x)=x\sin x$, $f\prime(x)=\sin x+x\cos x$. The graph marks the tangent as its base point moves.
pitfall: The derivative of a product is not the product of derivatives. Keep the numerator order in the quotient rule.
task: Move the tangent point and compare the two contributions to the product rule.
insight: A changing product has one contribution from each changing factor.

title: The chain rule
subtitle: Local rates multiply when one function feeds another.
definition: A composition changes in two stages: an input change first affects the inner function, then the outer function converts that change into an output change. The chain rule multiplies these local conversion rates.
conditions: $g$ is differentiable at $x$ and $f$ is differentiable at $g(x)$. The outer derivative must be evaluated at the inner output.
proof: Write the linear approximations $g(x+h)=g(x)+g\prime(x)h+o(h)$ and $f(u+k)=f(u)+f\prime(u)k+o(k)$. Substitution identifies the coefficient of $h$.
example: For $y=\sin(x^2)$, the inner rate is $2x$ and the outer rate is $\cos(x^2)$, giving $y\prime=2x\cos(x^2)$.
pitfall: Forgetting the inner derivative loses the change of scale. A naive proof that divides by $g(x+h)-g(x)$ needs care when it vanishes.
task: Move the input and observe how the tangent slope changes when the inner rate is zero.
insight: Local rates multiply when one function feeds another.

title: Implicit curves and related rates
subtitle: A constraint translates motion in one variable into motion in another.
definition: Implicit differentiation treats the dependent variable as a function while differentiating the whole equation. Related-rate problems instead differentiate a geometric constraint with respect to time, linking simultaneous motions.
conditions: A local differentiable graph $y(x)$ is needed for $\frac{dy}{dx}$. In the circle example the solved derivative requires $y\ne0$. Related rates must refer to the same instant and use consistent units.
proof: Apply the chain rule to $y(x)^2$. For a moving point, differentiating $x(t)^2+y(t)^2=4$ gives $x\dot x+y\dot y=0$.
example: At $(x,y)=(1,\sqrt3)$, the circle slope is $-1/\sqrt3$. If $\dot x=2$, then $\dot y=-2/\sqrt3$.
pitfall: Do not substitute instantaneous numerical values before differentiating: doing so can erase the varying quantities.
task: Move around the circle and inspect the tangent direction near its left and right edges.
insight: A constraint translates motion in one variable into motion in another.

title: Linear approximation and differentials
subtitle: The tangent predicts first-order change; curvature supplies the remainder.
definition: The tangent line is the first-order approximation to a differentiable function. A differential describes its predicted output change for a chosen input increment. The actual change generally includes a remainder.
conditions: The approximation improves locally; a rigorous finite error bound needs more information, such as a bound on the second derivative.
proof: Differentiability gives $f(a+h)=f(a)+f\prime(a)h+o(h)$. Dropping the remainder yields the linearization; it does not make the remainder equal zero.
example: For $f(x)=x^2$ at $a=1$, $f(1+h)=1+2h+h^2$. The tangent predicts $1+2h$, with exact error $h^2$.
pitfall: $dy$ and $\Delta y$ are generally unequal. An approximation sign carries mathematical information.
task: Shrink the increment and compare the curve, tangent and error segment.
insight: The tangent predicts first-order change; curvature supplies the remainder.

title: Extrema and critical points
subtitle: Extrema, critical candidates and endpoint comparison require different hypotheses.
definition: An absolute extremum compares a value with the entire domain; a local extremum compares it with values on some open interval around the point. A critical number lies in the domain and has derivative zero or no derivative. On a closed interval, endpoints are candidates alongside interior critical numbers.
conditions: The Extreme Value Theorem requires continuity on a closed bounded interval. Fermat's theorem requires a local extremum at an interior point and differentiability there. The closed-interval method relies on continuity on the full closed interval.
proof: At a differentiable local minimum, right difference quotients are nonnegative and left difference quotients are nonpositive; if their common limit exists, it is zero. Fermat gives a necessary condition only. The Extreme Value Theorem guarantees attainment, and the closed-interval method compares all interior critical values with both endpoint values.
example: For $f(x)=x^3-3x^2+1$ on $[-1/2,4]$, $f'(x)=3x(x-2)$, so the interior critical numbers are $0$ and $2$. The four candidate values are $1/8$, $1$, $-3$, and $17$; the absolute minimum is $-3$ at $2$, and the maximum is $17$ at $4.
pitfall: A horizontal tangent need not be an extremum ($x^3$ at zero); an extremum may occur where the derivative does not exist ($|x|$ at zero). A local extremum need not be absolute. Endpoints are checked separately.
task: List the interior critical numbers, evaluate them and both endpoints, then compare the values.
insight: Extrema, critical candidates and endpoint comparison require different hypotheses.

title: Rolle and the mean value theorem
subtitle: Rolle and the mean value theorem turn interval change into an interior derivative.
definition: For a continuous function on $[a,b]$ differentiable on $(a,b)$, the mean value theorem gives an interior derivative equal to the secant slope. Rolle's theorem is its zero-secant special case when $f(a)=f(b)$.
conditions: Require $a<b$, continuity on $[a,b]$, and differentiability on $(a,b)$; Rolle also requires equal endpoint values. Derivative-zero and equal-derivative consequences apply on an interval, not automatically across a disconnected domain.
proof: Subtract the secant line from f. The resulting function has equal endpoint values, so Rolle gives an interior zero derivative; rearranging recovers the secant slope. Applying MVT to arbitrary pairs proves that zero derivative means constant and equal derivatives mean a constant difference on an interval.
example: For $f(x)=x^3-x$ on $[0,2]$, the secant slope is $3$. Solving $3c^2-1=3$ gives $c=\frac{2}{\sqrt{3}}$, the only solution in $(0,2)$.
pitfall: Equal endpoint values do not suffice if interior differentiability fails. A domain that is not an interval can carry derivative zero everywhere on its domain without the function being globally constant.
task: Check each hypothesis before using Rolle or MVT; then solve the derivative-equals-secant equation inside the open interval.
insight: Rolle and the mean value theorem turn interval change into an interior derivative.

title: Shape from derivatives
subtitle: Slope and changing slope answer different questions about shape.
definition: The first derivative describes rise and fall. A sign change from positive to negative gives a local maximum; negative to positive gives a local minimum. The second derivative describes how the slope changes. An inflection point is where concavity changes.
conditions: For the first-derivative test, $f$ must be continuous on an interval containing $c$ and differentiable on either side of $c$. If $f'$ is positive just left of $c$ and negative just right, $f(c)$ is a local maximum; reversing the signs gives a local minimum. These are sufficient conditions, not necessary ones. For the second-derivative test, a sufficient assumption is that $f$ is twice continuously differentiable near $c$ and $f'(c)=0$. A positive $f''(c)$ gives a strict local minimum; a negative value gives a strict local maximum; zero is inconclusive.
proof: The mean value theorem turns a positive derivative on an interval into positive differences of function values. Applying the same idea to $f\prime$ explains concavity.
example: For $f=x^3-3x$, $f\prime=3x^2-3$ gives a local maximum at $-1$ and local minimum at $1$. Since $f\prime\prime=6x$, concavity changes at zero.
pitfall: $f\prime\prime(c)=0$ makes the second derivative test inconclusive. It does not automatically prove an inflection point. Continuity at the candidate is essential: set $f(x)=-|x|$ for $x\ne0$ and $f(0)=-1$. The derivative changes from positive to negative, but $0$ is a strict local minimum because nearby values exceed $-1$.
task: Locate the stationary points and the separate concavity-change point.
insight: Slope and changing slope answer different questions about shape.

title: Infinity and curve sketching
subtitle: Local derivative information and distant limits complete the same picture.
definition: A limit at infinity controls all sufficiently large inputs. Horizontal asymptotes describe finite limiting heights; a slant asymptote requires the difference from a line to tend to zero. A complete curve sketch combines domain, symmetry, intercepts, asymptotes, derivative signs and concavity.
conditions: A horizontal asymptote may differ at positive and negative infinity. For $y=mx+b$ to be asymptotic, require $f(x)-(mx+b)\to0$, not just a matching leading term in relative size.
proof: Divide rational expressions by the highest denominator power. In $(x^2+1)/x^2=1+1/x^2$, the remaining term tends to zero.
example: $f(x)=1+1/x^2$ has horizontal asymptote $y=1$ and a vertical asymptote at zero. It approaches the horizontal line from above.
pitfall: A curve may cross a horizontal asymptote. Infinity is a direction of limiting behaviour, not an endpoint in the domain.
task: Move farther from zero and compare the shrinking vertical gap with the asymptote.
insight: Local derivative information and distant limits complete the same picture.

title: Turn a constraint into an optimum
subtitle: The feasible domain is as important as the derivative.
definition: Optimization begins by identifying the quantity to optimize and its feasible domain. A constraint often removes a variable. Differentiate only after expressing the objective in terms of one independent variable, then compare all admissible candidates.
conditions: Boundary and degenerate cases belong to the problem unless explicitly excluded. Compactness and continuity can establish that a largest or smallest value exists.
proof: A rectangle of perimeter $P$ has sides $x$ and $P/2-x$. Its area has derivative $P/2-2x$ and second derivative $-2$, so its interior stationary point is the global maximum on the closed feasible interval.
example: For perimeter $8$, $A(x)=x(4-x)$ on $[0,4]$. The maximum is $4$ at $x=2$, a square; both endpoints have area zero.
pitfall: A critical number outside the feasible domain is irrelevant. A local test alone need not establish a global optimum on an unbounded domain.
task: Change the rectangle’s width while keeping its perimeter fixed.
insight: The feasible domain is as important as the derivative.

title: Newton’s tangent iteration
subtitle: Each tangent turns a nonlinear root problem into a linear one.
definition: Newton’s method replaces a function locally by its tangent line, then uses the tangent’s zero as the next estimate of a root. It is an iteration, not an algebraic identity for the root.
conditions: The derivative at each iterate must be nonzero. Fast local convergence needs a sufficiently close initial estimate and a suitably smooth function with a simple root.
proof: The tangent at $x_n$ is $y=f(x_n)+f\prime(x_n)(x-x_n)$. Setting this to zero and solving for $x$ gives the iteration.
example: For $f(x)=x^2-2$, the update is $(x_n+2/x_n)/2$. Starting at $2$ gives $1.5$, then about $1.4167$, approaching $\sqrt2$.
pitfall: Newton iterations can diverge, cycle or encounter a zero derivative. A plot and a small residual are not a universal convergence proof.
task: Move the starting point and inspect where its tangent meets the axis.
insight: Each tangent turns a nonlinear root problem into a linear one.

title: Recover a function from its rate
subtitle: A rate determines changes, but needs one value to determine position.
definition: An antiderivative of $f$ is a differentiable function $F$ with $F\prime=f$. On an interval, every antiderivative differs from any other by a constant. An initial condition chooses that constant.
conditions: The constant-difference conclusion requires a connected interval. Separate domain components can have independent constants.
proof: If $F\prime=G\prime$, the mean value theorem applied to $F-G$ shows that its value is constant between any two points of the interval.
example: If $s\prime(t)=2t$ and $s(0)=3$, then $s(t)=t^2+3$. Moving $C$ shifts the graph vertically without changing its slopes.
pitfall: An indefinite integral is a family of functions, not a number or an area.
task: Change the constant and observe which geometric properties stay the same.
insight: A rate determines changes, but needs one value to determine position.

title: Invert a function
subtitle: Inversion swaps inputs and outputs, so corresponding slopes are reciprocals.
definition: An inverse reverses a one-to-one function, exchanging its domain and range. Geometrically its graph reflects across $y=x$. A function that is not one-to-one may admit an inverse after restricting its domain.
conditions: For the derivative formula, the inverse exists locally, $f$ is differentiable there, and $f\prime$ at the corresponding input is nonzero.
proof: Differentiate $f(f^{-1}(y))=y$. The chain rule gives $f\prime(f^{-1}(y))(f^{-1})\prime(y)=1$, and division gives the reciprocal slope.
example: On $[0,\infty)$, the inverse of $x^2$ is $\sqrt{x}$. At corresponding positive points the slopes are $2x$ and $1/(2x)$.
pitfall: $f^{-1}$ means inverse function, not reciprocal. A domain restriction must be stated.

title: Exponential and logarithmic rates
subtitle: The natural exponential is its own rate of change.
definition: An exponential converts addition of inputs into multiplication of outputs. The natural base is the one whose rate equals its current value. The logarithm is its inverse and converts multiplication into addition. Logarithmic differentiation is useful for variable powers and products.
conditions: $\ln x$ requires $x>0$; $\ln|x|$ differentiates to $1/x$ on either interval avoiding zero. For $a^x$, require $a>0$ and its derivative is $a^x\ln a$.
proof: Using the inverse derivative formula for the exponential gives $(\ln x)\prime=1/e^{\ln x}=1/x$. The identity $a^x=e^{x\ln a}$ then gives the general exponential rule.
example: For $y=x^x$ with $x>0$, take logarithms: $\ln y=x\ln x$. Differentiating gives $y\prime/y=\ln x+1$, hence $y\prime=x^x(\ln x+1)$.
pitfall: Logarithms do not distribute over addition. Taking a logarithm can impose positivity restrictions.
task: Move along the exponential and compare its height with its tangent slope.
insight: The natural exponential is its own rate of change.

title: Indeterminate forms and L’Hôpital
subtitle: Check the form and hypotheses before replacing a ratio by a ratio of rates.
definition: L’Hôpital’s rule evaluates eligible indeterminate quotients by comparing derivative ratios. Products, differences and variable powers may first need algebraic or logarithmic conversion to a quotient of the right form.
conditions: Use a $0/0$ or infinite-over-infinite form. The numerator and denominator are differentiable in a deleted one-sided neighbourhood, the denominator derivative is nonzero, and the derivative ratio has the required finite or infinite limit.
proof: The Cauchy mean value theorem relates a quotient of function differences to a quotient of derivatives at an intermediate point. Passing to the limit under the rule’s hypotheses yields the conclusion.
example: For $\ln x/(x-1)$ as $x\to1$, the form is $0/0$. The derivative ratio is $1/x$, whose limit is $1$.
pitfall: Do not differentiate an arbitrary quotient’s numerator and denominator separately. If the derivative ratio has no limit, the rule may simply be inconclusive.
task: Approach zero and compare the exponential increment with its input increment.
insight: Check the form and hypotheses before replacing a ratio by a ratio of rates.

title: Antiderivatives form a family
subtitle: A derivative forgets vertical position.
definition: Antidifferentiation reverses differentiation. All antiderivatives on an interval differ by a constant; specifying one function value selects one member of the family.
conditions: Work on an interval. If the domain is disconnected, constants may be chosen separately on its components.
proof: For two antiderivatives $F,G$, $(F-G)\prime=0$. The mean value theorem on any subinterval gives equal endpoint values of $F-G$, so their difference is constant.
example: $F(x)=x^2+C$ satisfies $F\prime(x)=2x$. If $F(1)=4$, then $C=3$.
pitfall: The indefinite integral denotes functions. It is distinct from the definite integral, which is a signed number.
task: Vary the integration constant and compare the unchanged tangent slopes.
insight: A derivative forgets vertical position.

title: Accumulate with Riemann sums
subtitle: Tiny local contributions assemble into a finite total.
definition: A definite integral is the common limit of sums of signed rectangle areas as the partition mesh tends to zero, when that limit is independent of the sample choices. Positive heights add and negative heights subtract. Integrals are linear, additive over adjacent intervals and reverse sign when limits reverse.
conditions: A bounded function is Riemann integrable when its upper and lower sums can be made arbitrarily close. Continuous functions on a closed interval are integrable; finitely many ordinary jumps are allowed too.
proof: For $f(x)=x^2$ on $[0,1]$, right sums are $n^{-3}\sum i^2=(n+1)(2n+1)/(6n^2)$. Their limit is $1/3$; lower sums have the same limit.
example: The displayed right rectangles overestimate $x^2$ because the function increases. Increasing their number reduces the gap to $1/3$.
pitfall: An integral is signed accumulation, not necessarily geometric area. A few matching sums do not establish integrability.
task: Increase the rectangle count and compare the sum with the limiting value.
insight: Tiny local contributions assemble into a finite total.

title: The average value of a function
subtitle: An average replaces varying height with one equivalent constant height.
definition: The average height of an integrable function is its signed area divided by interval length. For a continuous function, at least one point reaches that average height: the mean value theorem for integrals.
conditions: Assume $a<b$ and integrability to define the average. Continuity on $[a,b]$ guarantees that the average is an attained value.
proof: The minimum and maximum bound the integral between $m(b-a)$ and $M(b-a)$. After division, the average lies in $[m,M]$; IVT supplies a point at that height.
example: For $x^2$ on $[0,b]$, the average is $b^2/3$. The matching point is $c=b/\sqrt3$.
pitfall: The average of the endpoint values is generally not the integral average.
task: Change the interval endpoint and compare the curve with its equal-area rectangle.
insight: An average replaces varying height with one equivalent constant height.

title: Differentiation meets accumulation
subtitle: The height of the next thin strip is the rate at which area grows.
definition: The first part of the fundamental theorem of calculus differentiates an accumulation function. The second evaluates a definite integral using any antiderivative: $\int_a^b f=F(b)-F(a)$. Together they connect a local rate with a total change.
conditions: For the standard course statement, $f$ is continuous on the closed interval. For evaluation, $F\prime=f$ on its interior with appropriate endpoint continuity.
proof: The quotient $[A(x+h)-A(x)]/h$ is an average of $f$ over a short interval. Continuity forces it to approach $f(x)$. Then $(A-F)\prime=0$, so endpoint subtraction gives the evaluation formula.
example: For $f(t)=t^2$, $A(x)=x^3/3$ and $A\prime(x)=x^2$. Increasing the upper limit adds a thin strip whose height is the current rate.
pitfall: A varying upper limit invokes the chain rule: $\frac{d}{dx}\bigl[\int_0^{g(x)}f(t)\,dt\bigr]=f(g(x))g\prime(x)$.
task: Move the upper limit and compare the accumulating area with the boundary height.
insight: The height of the next thin strip is the rate at which area grows.

title: Substitution changes the variable
subtitle: The differential compensates for a change of input scale.
definition: Substitution is the chain rule in reverse. The differential factor accounts for how rapidly the new variable changes. Definite-integral endpoints must describe the new variable.
conditions: The course rule assumes $g\prime$ continuous and $f$ continuous on the range involved. The signed one-variable rule can hold without monotonicity; oriented cancellation handles backtracking.
proof: If $F\prime=f$, then $(F\circ g)\prime=f(g)g\prime$. Applying FTC at the original endpoints gives $F(g(b))-F(g(a))$, which is the transformed integral.
example: $\int_0^1 2x\cos(x^2)dx=\int_0^1\cos u\,du=\sin1$ with $u=x^2$.
pitfall: Do not retain old bounds after changing variables. Every occurrence of the old variable must be accounted for.
task: Move the upper endpoint and compare the original and transformed accumulation.
insight: The differential compensates for a change of input scale.

title: Improper integrals are limits
subtitle: Infinite geometry can enclose finite accumulation.
definition: Infinite intervals and unbounded integrands are handled by limits of proper integrals. Each problematic endpoint or interior singularity gets its own limit. The improper integral converges only when all required limits are finite.
conditions: At an interior singularity split the integral there. On the whole real line split at a finite point; cancellation of divergent tails is not convergence.
proof: For $p\ne1$, $\int_1^R x^{-p}dx=(R^{1-p}-1)/(1-p)$. A finite limit exists exactly for $p>1$. At $p=1$ the integral is $\ln R$ and diverges.
example: $\int_1^\infty x^{-2}dx=1$, while $\int_0^1x^{-1/2}dx=2$. Near zero the power criterion reverses: $\int_0^1x^{-p}dx$ converges for $p<1$.
pitfall: An infinite height or interval does not automatically mean infinite area. Symmetric cancellation can conceal divergence.
task: Extend the cutoff for the reciprocal-square tail and compare with the limiting area.
insight: Infinite geometry can enclose finite accumulation.

title: Area between curves
subtitle: Choose slices whose boundaries are easiest to describe.
definition: Area is the integral of nonnegative slice height. With vertical slices, subtract lower curve from upper curve. With horizontal slices, subtract left boundary from right boundary.
conditions: Find intersections and split wherever the ordering changes. Boundaries should define a bounded measurable region; continuous piecewise boundaries suffice for the course setting.
proof: A narrow vertical rectangle has width $\Delta x$ and height $f(x)-g(x)$ when $f\ge g$. Summation and a limit give the integral.
example: Between $y=x$ and $y=x^2$ on $[0,1]$, $A=\int_0^1(x-x^2)dx=1/6$.
pitfall: Using one subtraction order across a crossing can cancel area.
task: Move the upper limit and inspect the region swept out between the curves.
insight: Choose slices whose boundaries are easiest to describe.

title: Volumes from cross-sections
subtitle: Volume is accumulated area, one thin slab at a time.
definition: A solid’s volume is the integral of cross-sectional area. Rotation around an axis produces disks or washers when slices are perpendicular to the axis. Radii are distances from the axis, not automatically coordinate values.
conditions: Use $0\le r(x)\le R(x)$ and valid bounds. The cross-sections must describe the solid without overlap in the slicing direction.
proof: A thin slab has approximate volume $A(x)\Delta x$. A washer’s area is the outer disk minus the inner disk, giving the difference of squared radii.
example: Rotating $0\le y\le x$ for $0\le x\le1$ around the horizontal axis gives $V=\pi\int_0^1x^2dx=\pi/3$.
pitfall: $\pi(R-r)^2$ is not a washer area. A shifted axis changes both radii.
task: Move the cross-section and compare its radius and area.
insight: Volume is accumulated area, one thin slab at a time.

title: Volumes from cylindrical shells
subtitle: A thin shell unwraps into an almost rectangular sheet.
definition: A strip parallel to the rotation axis sweeps out a thin shell. Its leading volume is circumference times height times thickness. Shells often avoid solving an inverse function needed by washers.
conditions: The radius is nonnegative distance to the axis. The shells must cover the target solid once; split regions if one radius corresponds to overlapping strips.
proof: The annular area difference is $\pi[(r+\Delta r)^2-r^2]=2\pi r\Delta r+\pi(\Delta r)^2$. The second-order term disappears in the limit.
example: Rotating the region under $y=x$ on $[0,1]$ about the vertical axis gives $2\pi\int_0^1x^2dx=2\pi/3$.
pitfall: Shells and washers for different axes describe different solids. Choose orientation before writing a formula.
task: Move the shell radius and observe circumference times height.
insight: A thin shell unwraps into an almost rectangular sheet.

title: Integration by parts
subtitle: The product rule becomes an exchange between two integrals.
definition: Integration by parts transfers a derivative from one factor to another. It is especially useful when differentiating one factor simplifies it, while integrating the other remains manageable. Repeated application or an equation involving the original integral may be needed.
conditions: For the standard definite formula, use continuously differentiable functions on the interval. Keep boundary terms in definite integrals and constants in indefinite results.
proof: Integrate the product rule $(uv)\prime=u\prime v+uv\prime$, then rearrange. The boundary version is $\int_a^buv\prime=[uv]_a^b-\int_a^bu\prime v$.
example: Choose $u=x$, $dv=e^x dx$. Then $du=dx$, $v=e^x$, and $\int xe^x dx=xe^x-e^x+C$.
pitfall: Choosing factors mechanically can make the new integral harder. Verify the final answer by differentiation.
task: Move the upper endpoint and compare the integral with its boundary term minus the simpler integral.
insight: The product rule becomes an exchange between two integrals.

title: Trigonometric integrals
subtitle: Use symmetry and identities to expose a familiar differential.
definition: For powers of sine and cosine, save a factor matching a differential when an exponent is odd, then convert the remaining even power. When both exponents are even, use half-angle identities. Tangent-secant products use analogous identities.
conditions: Trigonometric substitutions and identities must respect the real domain. Radian measure is assumed.
proof: For an odd sine power, isolate $\sin x\,dx$ and set $u=\cos x$. Replace $\sin^2x$ by $1-u^2$. Even powers are reduced using double-angle identities.
example: $\int\sin^3x\cos^2x\,dx=-\int(1-u^2)u^2du=-u^3/3+u^5/5+C$, with $u=\cos x$.
pitfall: An identity may simplify an integrand without immediately producing a matching differential.
task: Change the upper limit and see the signed accumulation of $\sin^2x$.
insight: Use symmetry and identities to expose a familiar differential.

title: Substitute a triangle
subtitle: A right triangle converts an algebraic radical into a geometric coordinate.
definition: Trigonometric substitution replaces a radical using a Pythagorean identity. Standard choices are $a\sin\theta$ for $\sqrt{a^2-x^2}$, $a\tan\theta$ for $\sqrt{a^2+x^2}$, and $a\sec\theta$ for $\sqrt{x^2-a^2}$.
conditions: Assume $a>0$ and choose a parameter interval that fixes the relevant signs and makes the substitution one-to-one. The first displayed identity uses $-\pi/2\le\theta\le\pi/2$.
proof: After $x=a\sin\theta$, the radicand becomes $a^2(1-\sin^2\theta)=a^2\cos^2\theta$. The chosen interval removes the absolute value.
example: For $\int dx/\sqrt{1-x^2}$, put $x=\sin\theta$. The differential cancels the radical, giving $\theta+C=\arcsin x+C$ on $(-1,1)$.
pitfall: $\sqrt{\cos^2\theta}=|\cos\theta|$, not always $\cos\theta$.
task: Move the angle and compare the horizontal projection with the circle’s vertical height.
insight: A right triangle converts an algebraic radical into a geometric coordinate.

title: Split a rational function
subtitle: Algebra decomposes a difficult integral into standard pieces.
definition: Polynomial division first separates an improper rational function into a polynomial plus a proper fraction. Factor the denominator over the reals, then use constants over linear powers and linear numerators over irreducible quadratic powers.
conditions: Keep all original denominator exclusions. Repeated factors require a term for every power up to their multiplicity.
proof: Multiply the proposed decomposition by the common denominator and equate polynomial coefficients. The resulting linear system fixes the numerators.
example: $1/[x(x+1)]=1/x-1/(x+1)$ since $(x+1)-x=1$. Thus its integral is $\ln|x|-\ln|x+1|+C$ on an interval avoiding $-1,0$.
pitfall: Leaving out lower powers of a repeated factor gives an incomplete ansatz.
task: Move a positive input and compare the rational value with the difference of its simpler fractions.
insight: Algebra decomposes a difficult integral into standard pieces.

title: Midpoint and trapezoidal rules
subtitle: Curvature controls how much straight-edged approximations miss.
definition: Midpoint rectangles sample the centre of each interval. Trapezoids connect endpoint heights by straight segments. Both approximate integrals using finitely many function evaluations; smoothness bounds can certify the error.
conditions: For the stated bounds, $|f\prime\prime|\le K$ on the whole interval and the rules use equal widths. The source proof is beyond the syllabus.

title: Simpson’s parabolic rule
subtitle: Curved approximations can gain accuracy much faster than straight ones.
definition: For even $n$, Simpson’s composite rule uses weights $1,4,2,4,\ldots,2,4,1$ with factor $h/3$. The source derives it as a weighted average of trapezoid and midpoint rules on paired panels.
conditions: The panel count $n$ must be even. If $|f^{(4)}|\le K$ on the whole interval, the source states $|E_S|\le K(b-a)^5/(180n^4)$ and does not prove the bound.
proof: The source derives the composite formula from $S_n=\frac13T_{n/2}+\frac23M_{n/2}$. It states the fourth-derivative error bound without proof.
example: For $f(x)=x^4$ on $[0,1]$, Simpson’s value is $1/5+2/(15n^4)$. Doubling $n$ divides this error by $16$.
pitfall: Using an odd number of equal subintervals does not fit the composite formula.
task: Double the even interval count and compare the error’s rate of decrease.
insight: Curved approximations can gain accuracy much faster than straight ones.

title: Sequences and their limits
subtitle: Convergence is a guarantee about all sufficiently late terms.
definition: A sequence assigns a real value to each positive integer. Convergence means every sufficiently late term lies inside any chosen tolerance band. Finitely many early terms do not affect the limit.
conditions: The index is an integer. The chosen $N$ must control the entire tail, not just one subsequence or a finite displayed window.
proof: For $a_n=1/n$, given $\varepsilon>0$, choose $N>1/\varepsilon$. Then $n>N$ implies $0<a_n<\varepsilon$.
example: $a_n=1+(-1)^n/n$ oscillates around $1$ with shrinking amplitude and converges to $1$.
pitfall: A bounded sequence need not converge. A small difference between successive terms alone also does not prove convergence.
task: Increase the number of visible terms and inspect the narrowing tail.
insight: Convergence is a guarantee about all sufficiently late terms.

title: Subsequences expose divergence
subtitle: A divergent sequence can hide several different limiting behaviours.
definition: A subsequence selects terms using strictly increasing indices. Every subsequence of a convergent sequence has the same limit. Consequently, two subsequences with different limits prove divergence. Every convergent sequence is bounded.
conditions: The indices must tend to infinity. Repeating a fixed term is not a subsequence in this sense.
proof: For any tail threshold $N$, eventually $n_k>N$, so the original convergence estimate also controls the selected terms. Boundedness follows by combining a bounded tail with the finite initial segment.
example: For $a_n=(-1)^n$, even-index terms equal $1$ and odd-index terms equal $-1$. They have different limits, so the full sequence diverges.
pitfall: One convergent subsequence does not prove convergence of the original sequence.
task: Inspect the even and odd terms separately as more terms are added.
insight: A divergent sequence can hide several different limiting behaviours.

title: Calculate sequence limits
subtitle: The same limit principles apply to a discrete domain.
definition: Sequence limits obey algebraic laws, squeezing and continuity under composition. A function limit at infinity can establish a sequence limit by restricting inputs to integers. Geometric sequences have behaviour determined by their ratio.
conditions: Quotient limits need a nonzero limiting denominator. The continuous-function rule requires continuity at the limiting input. L’Hôpital applies to a differentiable real extension, not directly to the integer sequence.
proof: Divide numerator and denominator by $n$ to get $1/(1+1/n)$. Since $1/n\to0$ and the denominator stays away from zero, the limit is $1$.
example: For $|r|<1$, $r^n\to0$. For $r=1$ the sequence is constant, while $r=-1$ oscillates and $r>1$ grows without bound.
pitfall: The existence of a sequence limit does not force an arbitrary interpolating function to have a limit at infinity.
task: Compare shrinking alternating deviations with the fixed limiting height.
insight: The same limit principles apply to a discrete domain.

title: Monotone and bounded
subtitle: One direction plus a barrier forces a finite destination.
definition: A monotone sequence moves in one direction. If it is also bounded in that direction, it converges. This is especially useful for recursively defined sequences whose limit is difficult to see explicitly.
conditions: Both monotonicity and boundedness must be proved. A fixed point of a recurrence is only a candidate limit until convergence is established.
proof: Let $L$ be the supremum. For every $\varepsilon>0$, some term exceeds $L-\varepsilon$; all later terms do too by monotonicity, while none exceeds $L$.
example: $a_n=1-2^{-n}$ increases and is bounded above by $1$, so it converges to $1$.
pitfall: A monotone unbounded sequence does not converge to a real number.

title: A series is a sequence of sums
subtitle: Infinite addition is defined through finite sums and a limit.
definition: A series converges when its partial sums converge to a finite number. Geometric series have a constant term ratio. Telescoping series expose cancellation after writing out a finite partial sum.
conditions: The geometric formula requires $|r|<1$. Derive the finite sum first, then take its limit. Indexing determines the first term.
proof: If $S_N=1+r+\cdots+r^{N-1}$, then $S_N-rS_N=1-r^N$. Hence $S_N=(1-r^N)/(1-r)$ and $r^N\to0$ when $|r|<1$.
example: $\sum_{n=1}^\infty1/[n(n+1)]$ telescopes because $1/[n(n+1)]=1/n-1/(n+1)$. The partial sum is $1-1/(N+1)$, giving total $1$.
pitfall: The terms and the partial sums are different sequences. A series is not evaluated by simply taking the term limit.
task: Add more geometric terms and compare the remaining gap with the total.
insight: Infinite addition is defined through finite sums and a limit.

title: The term test only rules out
subtitle: Small terms can still accumulate without bound.
definition: Convergent partial sums force their successive differences, the terms, to vanish. Therefore terms that fail to approach zero prove divergence. The converse is false. Linear combinations of convergent series behave as expected.
conditions: Use the contrapositive as a divergence test. If the term limit is zero, more information is needed.
proof: Writing $a_n=S_n-S_{n-1}$, convergence of both partial sums to the same sum gives $a_n\to0$. The harmonic series shows why the reverse implication fails.
example: Group $1/n$ in blocks from $2^{k-1}+1$ to $2^k$. Each block has $2^{k-1}$ terms of size at least $1/2^k$, so contributes at least $1/2$.
pitfall: Terms tending to zero do not make the total finite. Very slow divergence may look flat in a finite plot.
task: Increase the cutoff and watch harmonic partial sums keep growing.
insight: Small terms can still accumulate without bound.

title: Compare a series with an area
subtitle: Discrete rectangles and continuous area control one another.
definition: The integral test compares positive decreasing terms with rectangles over a continuous curve. The series and its associated improper integral either both converge or both diverge. Integral tails also bound the remainder.

title: Direct and limit comparison
subtitle: Choose a benchmark that captures the dominant size of the terms.
definition: Direct comparison transfers convergence downwards and divergence upwards for nonnegative terms. Limit comparison says positive series have the same behaviour when their term ratio tends to a positive finite number.
conditions: Comparison inequalities must hold eventually in the needed direction. The usual two-way limit comparison needs $0<L<\infty$.
proof: Nonnegative partial sums of the smaller series are increasing and bounded by the convergent larger total. For limit comparison, eventually $L/2<a_n/b_n<3L/2$, reducing it to direct comparison.
example: $1/(n^2+1)\le1/n^2$, so the first series converges. Also $[1/(n^2+1)]/[1/n^2]\to1$.
pitfall: A convergent smaller series tells nothing about a larger one. A ratio limit of zero or infinity needs a one-way argument.
task: Compare both positive term sequences as the index grows.
insight: Choose a benchmark that captures the dominant size of the terms.

title: Absolute and conditional convergence
subtitle: Cancellation can produce convergence that absolute size cannot.
definition: Absolute convergence means the sum of absolute values is finite and implies convergence. Conditional convergence means the signed series converges while its absolute-value series diverges. Alternating terms with decreasing magnitudes tending to zero converge and have a useful remainder bound.
conditions: For the alternating test, $b_n\ge0$, $b_n$ is eventually nonincreasing and $b_n\to0$. Apply the bound after monotonicity begins.
proof: Even partial sums increase and odd partial sums decrease, enclosing one another. Their gap is a term tending to zero, so both subsequences share a limit.
example: $1-1/2+1/3-\cdots$ converges conditionally to $\ln2$. Its absolute series is harmonic and diverges; after $N$ terms the error is at most $1/(N+1)$.
pitfall: Alternating signs alone are insufficient. Rearranging a conditionally convergent series can change its sum.
task: Watch partial sums alternate above and below their limiting level.
insight: Cancellation can produce convergence that absolute size cannot.

title: Ratio and root tests
subtitle: These tests look for exponential-scale decay.
definition: The ratio test detects eventual geometric shrinkage and is useful with factorials or exponentials. The root test measures exponential size directly through $|a_n|^{1/n}$. A limit below one gives absolute convergence; above one gives divergence.
conditions: The ratio must be defined eventually. These course limit versions assume the relevant limit exists. If it equals one, the test is inconclusive.
proof: Choose $q$ strictly between the limit and one. Eventually each magnitude is at most $q$ times its predecessor, giving a convergent geometric bound. The root test bounds $|a_n|$ directly by $q^n$.
example: For $a_n=1/n!$, the ratio is $1/(n+1)\to0$. For both $1/n$ and $1/n^2$, the ratio tends to one although only the second series converges.
pitfall: A test limit of one is not a verdict. Try a comparison or integral test instead.
task: Compare factorial-decaying terms with a geometric benchmark.
insight: These tests look for exponential-scale decay.

title: Power series and their radius
subtitle: A power series is a local representation with a domain of validity.
definition: A power series is a series of monomials $\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}a_n(x-c)^n$. Its finite partial sums are polynomials; the series itself is not a polynomial unless only finitely many coefficients are nonzero. Its sum function is defined only at inputs where the series converges. The radius gives convergence in the open interval around c; each finite endpoint requires its own test.
conditions: The radius may be zero or infinite. A ratio-test calculation determines the open interval, not automatically either endpoint.
proof: If convergence holds at one noncentral point, comparison with a geometric series gives absolute convergence at every closer point. The boundary of all such distances defines the radius.
example: $\sum_{n=0}^\infty x^n=1/(1-x)$ for $|x|<1$. Both endpoints fail because the terms do not tend to zero.
pitfall: Do not include endpoints solely because an inequality was written with equality during a radius calculation.
task: Move $x$ towards the radius and observe how slowly finite sums settle.
insight: A power series is a local representation with a domain of validity.

title: Differentiate and integrate a series
subtitle: One known series can generate a family of useful representations.
definition: Inside its radius, a power series can be differentiated and integrated term by term. The resulting series have the same radius, though endpoint convergence can change. Substituting, scaling and combining known series builds new representations.
conditions: Work strictly inside the common interval of convergence for the termwise theorem. Recheck endpoints separately afterward.
proof: On each smaller closed interval, geometric comparison controls the tails uniformly; this justifies exchanging the limit with integration. The corresponding theorem for derivatives yields the differentiated series.
example: Integrating the geometric series from zero to $x$ gives $-\ln(1-x)=\sum_{n=1}^\infty x^n/n$ for $|x|<1$.
pitfall: The same radius does not mean the same closed interval of convergence. Infinite series are not unrestricted polynomials.
task: Compare finite geometric sums near and far from the centre.
insight: One known series can generate a family of useful representations.

title: Taylor polynomials and remainder
subtitle: Coefficients build the approximation; the remainder certifies it.
definition: Taylor coefficients match successive derivatives at a centre. The remainder decides whether higher-degree polynomials converge to the function. Maclaurin series are centred at zero. Smoothness alone does not guarantee equality with the Taylor series.
conditions: Taylor’s finite remainder theorem needs the stated derivatives on the interval between $a$ and $x$. To conclude equality with an infinite series, prove $R_n(x)\to0$.
proof: If a power-series representation exists, differentiating repeatedly at the centre isolates each coefficient as $f^{(k)}(a)/k!$. The remainder bound $|R_n(x)|\le M|x-a|^{n+1}/(n+1)!$ certifies finite approximation when $M$ bounds the next derivative.
example: For $e^x$, all derivatives equal $e^x$, so $T_n(x)=\sum_{k=0}^nx^k/k!$. On $|x|\le1$, the remainder is at most $e/(n+1)!$, which tends to zero.
pitfall: A formal Taylor series may fail to represent a smooth function. Matching finitely many derivatives is only local information.
task: Increase the degree and compare the polynomial with the exponential away from the centre.
insight: Coefficients build the approximation; the remainder certifies it.

title: The general binomial series
subtitle: Generalized binomial coefficients extend a familiar finite pattern.
definition: The binomial theorem extends from nonnegative integer powers to real exponents using Taylor coefficients. The generalized coefficient is $k(k-1)\cdots(k-n+1)/n!$, with zeroth coefficient one.
conditions: For a general real exponent the standard open interval is $|x|<1$. Nonnegative integer exponents terminate and give polynomials valid everywhere. Other endpoints need separate analysis.
proof: Repeated differentiation gives $f^{(n)}(0)=k(k-1)\cdots(k-n+1)$. Taylor’s theorem and convergence arguments identify the function on the permitted interval.
example: $\sqrt{1+x}=1+x/2-x^2/8+x^3/16-\cdots$. At $x=0.1$, the quadratic approximation is $1.04875$.
pitfall: The coefficient is not $k^n/n!$. Far outside the convergence interval, adding terms need not improve an approximation.

title: Extract a limit from a series
subtitle: The first surviving term reveals the hidden scale of a limit.
definition: A justified local expansion exposes the first nonzero term after cancellation. That term determines the scale and limiting coefficient. The remainder must be smaller than the denominator’s scale.
conditions: Use an expansion valid in a neighbourhood and retain enough terms. A remainder of order $O(x^3)$ cannot determine a quotient’s cubic coefficient.
proof: Write $\sin x=x-x^3/6+O(x^5)$. Subtract $x$ and divide by $x^3$ to get $-1/6+O(x^2)$, which tends to $-1/6$.
example: Likewise, $e^x=1+x+x^2/2+O(x^3)$ gives $\lim_{x\to0}(e^x-1-x)/x^2=1/2$.
pitfall: Cancelling leading terms without controlling the remainder can produce an unjustified limit.
task: Approach zero and compare the scaled sine remainder with $-1/6$.
insight: The first surviving term reveals the hidden scale of a limit.

title: Vectors in space
subtitle: Coordinates describe a point; a vector describes a displacement.
definition: A point is a location. A free vector is an equivalence class of directed segments with the same length and direction. Choosing an origin identifies its position vector with coordinates. The displacement from $A$ to $B$ is $B-A$. Addition follows the triangle or parallelogram law; scalar multiplication scales length and may reverse direction. In $\mathbb R^3$, $(a,b,c)=a\mathbf i+b\mathbf j+c\mathbf k$.
conditions: The coordinate axes are orthonormal and oriented by the right-hand rule. The angle formula assumes both vectors are nonzero; the coordinate dot product also works for zero vectors.
proof: Coordinate addition gives commutativity and associativity, a zero vector and additive inverses. Distributing real multiplication gives the two distributive laws, $(st)\mathbf u=s(t\mathbf u)$ and $1\mathbf u=\mathbf u$. Expanding $\|\mathbf u-\mathbf v\|^2$ and comparing with the cosine rule yields the dot-product angle formula.
example: With $\mathbf u=(1,0,0)$ and $\mathbf v=(\cos\theta,\sin\theta,0)$, the vectors have unit length and $\mathbf u\cdot\mathbf v=\cos\theta$. Their sum is the parallelogram diagonal.
pitfall: A position vector depends on the origin. A displacement does not. A zero dot product means perpendicularity only when both vectors are nonzero.
task: Rotate the second unit vector. Predict the sign of the dot product before it passes through a right angle.
insight: The dot product turns geometric alignment into a scalar. The norm satisfies $\|\mathbf u\|=\sqrt{\mathbf u\cdot\mathbf u}$.

title: A curve and its clock
subtitle: The same geometric path can have many parametrizations.
definition: A parametrized curve is a continuous map from an interval into $\mathbb R^2$ or $\mathbb R^3$; its image is the geometric curve. A vector-valued map is continuous exactly when its components are continuous. A parametrization records order, speed and possible repetitions that its image alone does not record.
conditions: To cover the same complete image, $\phi:J\to I$ must be continuous and onto the original parameter interval. For differentiable reparametrizations, $\mathbf s'(u)=\mathbf r'(\phi(u))\phi'(u)$.
proof: The image identity follows from surjectivity: every parameter $t\in I$ equals $\phi(u)$ for some $u$. The componentwise one-variable chain rule gives the derivative formula. An increasing clock preserves traversal direction; a decreasing clock reverses it.
example: The displayed helix makes one turn when $t$ increases by $2\pi$ and rises by $2\pi$. On the whole real line, replacing $t$ by $u^3$ preserves its image but gives zero velocity at $u=0$.
pitfall: A singular parametrization need not describe a singular geometric curve. Also, continuity alone is extremely weak: a Peano curve can have the entire unit square as its image.
task: Trace the helix and compare equal changes in the parameter with changes in position. Explain what changes under $t=u^3$.
insight: Geometry is the image; parametrization is the way the image is visited.

title: Build a parametrization
subtitle: Lines, circles, ellipses, cycloids and helices from geometry.
definition: A line has the affine parametrization $\mathbf p+t\mathbf v$ with $\mathbf v\ne0$. A circle is $(a+R\cos t,b+R\sin t)$, and an ellipse is $(A\cos t,B\sin t)$. A helix adds a height changing with angle. A cycloid is the trajectory of a point on the rim of a circle rolling without slipping.
conditions: Use $R,A,B>0$. An interval of length $2\pi$ covers a circle or ellipse; the cycloid formula uses a circle rolling along the horizontal axis without slipping. The parameter domain is part of the specification.
proof: For the cycloid, the center is $(Rt,R)$ and the radius vector to the marked point is $(-R\sin t,-R\cos t)$. Adding gives the formula. Eliminating $t$ from the ellipse gives $x^2/A^2+y^2/B^2=1$, because $\cos^2t+\sin^2t=1$. Conversely every point of that ellipse has such an angle.
example: For $\mathbf r(t)=(t^2+t,t^2-t)$, $x-y=2t$ and $x+y=2t^2$, hence $(x-y)^2=2(x+y)$. Conversely set $t=(x-y)/2$ to recover both coordinates.
pitfall: Eliminating a parameter can introduce points that the chosen parameter interval never visits. Verify both containment directions and the permitted parameter range.
task: Switch curve families and traverse the displayed parameter interval. Identify which curves close and which do not. For the cycloid, relate the moving point to the rolling circle.
insight: Constructing a parametrization is a geometric decomposition problem; deriving an implicit equation is an elimination problem.

title: Tangents, velocity and singularities
subtitle: A derivative controls motion; its failure needs geometric care.
formula: \begin{gathered}\mathbf v=\mathbf r'\\\text{speed}=\|\mathbf r'\|\\\mathbf a=\mathbf r''\\T(\lambda)=\mathbf r(t_0)+\lambda\mathbf r'(t_0)\end{gathered}
definition: The tangent vector is the limit of secant displacement divided by parameter change. A parametrization is regular at $t_0$ when this derivative exists and is nonzero. Otherwise it is singular there. If the parameter is time, its first and second derivatives are velocity and acceleration. Each regular visit to a point induces a tangent line.
conditions: The tangent-line formula requires $\mathbf r'(t_0)\ne0$. At a self-intersection, different parameter values may induce different lines. Endpoint and one-sided tangents need a separate one-sided definition.
proof: For the helix, $\mathbf r'=(-\sin t,\cos t,1)$, $\|\mathbf r'\|=\sqrt2$ and $\mathbf r''=(-\cos t,-\sin t,0)$. Thus its tangent never vanishes. For the cusp $x^2=y^3$, any differentiable parametrization through the origin at an interior time has $y'=0$ because $y\ge0$ has a local minimum; $x^2=y^3$ then forces $x'=0$.
example: The cusp admits $\mathbf c(t)=(t^3,t^2)$. Its derivative vanishes at zero, yet $x/y=t\to0$ shows that secant lines approach the vertical axis, its geometric tangent.
pitfall: A zero derivative does not by itself rule out a geometric tangent, and acceleration need not point in the direction of motion.
task: Move the parameter and compare the tangent arrow with the local curve direction. Derive a nearby secant vector $r(t+h)-r(t)$ on paper, then explain its limiting direction.
insight: Regularity makes the first-order tangent construction reliable. Singular cases must be examined using the curve itself.

title: Surfaces and level sets
subtitle: A height graph and its horizontal slices encode the same function.
definition: Write $G_f$ for the graph of $f$. For $f:D\subseteq\mathbb R^2\to\mathbb R$, its graph is $\{(x,y,f(x,y)):(x,y)\in D\}$. A level set $f^{-1}(c)$ lies in the input plane; the corresponding horizontal intersection of the graph lies in the plane $z=c$. A contour plot overlays selected level sets, often separated by a constant difference in height.
conditions: Always specify the real domain before plotting. Denominators must be nonzero, logarithm arguments positive and even-root arguments nonnegative. A level set may be empty, a point, disconnected or fail to be a regular curve.
proof: For the paraboloid, setting $z=c$ gives a circle of radius $\sqrt c$ when $c>0$, the origin when $c=0$, and no points when $c<0$. Projecting the intersection vertically produces the contour in the input plane.
example: The upper hemisphere $f(x,y)=\sqrt{36-x^2-y^2}$ has domain $x^2+y^2\le36$ and, for $0\le c\le6$, contours $x^2+y^2=36-c^2$. The expression $x/\sqrt{y^2-x}$ instead requires $y^2>x$.
pitfall: A level curve is a subset of the domain; it is not the entire horizontal plane. A graph cannot have two different output heights at the same input.
task: Move the slice height and predict the contour radius. Compare equal height intervals with the changing spacing of contours.
insight: Dense contours correspond to rapid height change in the direction transverse to them.

title: Distance and neighborhoods
subtitle: The language needed to quantify “nearby”.
formula: \begin{gathered}d(\mathbf x,\mathbf p)=\|\mathbf x-\mathbf p\|_2\\B_\delta(\mathbf p)=\{\mathbf x:d(\mathbf x,\mathbf p)<\delta\}\end{gathered}
definition: Euclidean distance is the norm of the displacement. A point $p$ is a limit point of $S$ if every punctured ball $B_\delta(p)\setminus\{p\}$ meets $S$. A set is open if each of its points has a ball contained in the set. It is closed if it contains all its limit points; equivalently its complement is open.
conditions: Openness and closedness are relative to an ambient space, here $\mathbb R^n$. A limit point need not belong to $S$. Being open and being closed are not opposite exhaustive possibilities.
proof: Distance satisfies identity of indiscernibles, symmetry and the triangle inequality. Those three axioms already force nonnegativity: $0=d(x,x)\le d(x,y)+d(y,x)=2d(x,y)$. An isolated point has a small ball containing no other point of the set, so it fails the punctured-ball test.
example: The disk $x^2+y^2<1$ is open but not closed; the disk $x^2+y^2\le1$ is closed but not open. The origin is not a limit point of the unit circle. Every real number is a limit point of $\mathbb Q$.
pitfall: A point belonging to a set does not automatically make it a limit point. A finite set has no limit points in $\mathbb R^n$.
task: Move the probe $p=(s,0)$ toward the boundary. Compare the fixed neighborhood radius $1/4$ with the available distance $1-|s|$. Explain when a smaller neighborhood would fit.
insight: The same ball quantifier underlies topology, limits, continuity and differentiability.

title: The $\varepsilon$–$\delta$ limit
subtitle: One radius must control every nearby input.
definition: A limit $L$ controls the outputs for all sufficiently close inputs, excluding the target point itself. A restricted limit uses inputs from a specified subset $S\subseteq D$. This same definition works for scalar or vector outputs by using the corresponding Euclidean norm.
conditions: The point $p$ must be a limit point of the set of permitted inputs. The value $f(p)$ may be absent or unrelated to the limit. The chosen $\delta$ may depend on $\varepsilon$, but cannot depend on which nearby point or approach direction is selected.
proof: For $f(x,y)=x^2+y^2$ at zero, choose $\delta=\sqrt\varepsilon$: then $0<\sqrt{x^2+y^2}<\delta$ implies $|f(x,y)|<\varepsilon$. For a vector map, component convergence is equivalent to vector convergence because $|v_i|\le\|v\|\le\sqrt n\max_i|v_i|$.
example: A vector example is $\lim_{t\to0^+}(t^t,(\cos t-1)/t^2)=(1,-1/2)$: $t\log t\to0$ gives the first component and the cosine limit gives the second.
pitfall: Testing a finite collection of paths is not an existence proof. The universal quantifier covers every point in the punctured ball.

title: Why a limit does not exist
subtitle: Two incompatible approaches are enough.
definition: If a multivariable limit exists, every restriction to a set approaching the same point has that limit. Therefore two different restricted limits, or one restriction without a limit, disprove existence.
conditions: The paths must lie in the function domain away from the target and actually approach it. Here $D=\mathbb R^2\setminus\{(0,0)\}$ and $r>0$.
proof: Along $y=0$, the value is zero. Along $y=x$, the value is $1/2$ at every nonzero point. These cannot both tend to the same real number. In polar coordinates, the height depends only on angle, so shrinking the radius cannot remove the disagreement.
example: At angles $0,\pi/4,\pi/2,3\pi/4$, the respective heights are $0,1/2,0,-1/2$. Both coordinate-axis tests pass with zero and still miss the diagonal obstruction.
pitfall: Agreement on the two axes proves nothing about existence. Defining $f(0,0)$ cannot repair an absent limit.
task: Choose the exact angles $0$ and $\pi/4$. Compare the ray heights. Explain algebraically why approaching the origin along either displayed ray cannot change its height.
insight: Nonexistence needs a counterexample to uniformity; two paths provide a particularly clear one.

title: When every line is misleading
subtitle: A curved approach can reveal what straight lines conceal.
definition: Approaching along every straight line still need not determine a multivariable limit. The displayed function is a coordinate-swapped version of the lecture example. Its denominator suggests balancing $x^4$ against $y^2$, leading to parabolic paths.

title: Squeeze, extend, compose
subtitle: A bound proves what pictures can only suggest.
definition: The squeeze theorem transfers a common limit from lower and upper bounds to the function between them. A map is continuous at $p$ when nearby inputs give outputs close to $f(p)$. At a domain limit point this is equivalent to $\lim_{x\to p}f(x)=f(p)$; continuity is automatic at isolated domain points.
conditions: The bounding inequalities must hold for every sufficiently close allowed input. Sum, scalar-multiple, product and quotient limit laws require the component limits, and a quotient additionally requires a nonzero limiting denominator.
proof: The displayed bound tends to zero uniformly as $(x,y)\to0$, proving the limit zero. Setting the missing origin value to zero makes the function continuous there. Polynomial maps are continuous; rational maps are continuous wherever their denominators are nonzero. Continuous compositions and vector componentwise continuity follow directly from the neighborhood definition.
example: The extension $g(0,0)=0$ of $g(x,y)=x^4/(x^2+y^2)$ is continuous because $0\le g\le x^2+y^2$. A composition such as $e^{x^2yz^3}$ is continuous on $\mathbb R^3$. Dot products of continuous vector maps are continuous.
pitfall: A formula undefined at the target is not itself continuous there. First establish the limit, then specify an extension value. Changing the value cannot fix a limit that fails to exist.

title: Infinity means every escape route
subtitle: Leaving every bounded set is stronger than moving along one axis.
definition: A limit at infinity requires that for each $\varepsilon>0$, all permitted inputs beyond some radius $N$ have output distance less than $\varepsilon$ from the proposed limit. Thus $\|\mathbf x\|\to\infty$ allows escape in every direction, with directions changing along the way.
conditions: The input domain must be unbounded. The symbol $\infty$ here is a norm condition, not the positive end of each coordinate axis.
proof: For the displayed function the absolute value is at most $1/r$, where $r=\sqrt{x^2+y^2}$. Taking $N>1/\varepsilon$ proves the limit. Consequently $(x/(x^2+y^2),-1)\to(0,-1)$ componentwise.
example: Although $\lim_{x\to+\infty}\lim_{y\to+\infty}e^{-(x+y)}=0$, its norm-infinity limit fails: on $(t,0)$ it tends to zero, while on $(-t,0)$ it grows without bound as $t\to+\infty$.
pitfall: An iterated coordinate limit can exist when the genuine multivariable limit does not. Increasing both coordinates is only one kind of escape.
task: Expand the exclusion radius and inspect the remaining surface. Relate the maximum possible magnitude to $1/N$.
insight: A limit at infinity is uniform control outside a large ball.

title: Partial derivatives are slice slopes
subtitle: Freeze one input and recover ordinary calculus.
definition: The $x$-partial derivative differentiates the slice with $y$ fixed; the $y$-partial fixes $x$. At the graph point $(a,b,f(a,b))$, their slice tangent vectors are $(1,0,f_x)$ and $(0,1,f_y)$. Partial derivatives are functions whose domains can be smaller than the original domain.
conditions: Use an interior point, or specify appropriate one-sided boundary derivatives. The difference-quotient limits must exist; a symbolic formula valid away from a piecewise junction does not settle derivatives at that junction.
proof: For the paraboloid, $f(a+h,b)-f(a,b)=2ah+h^2$, so division by $h$ and passage to the limit gives $f_x(a,b)=2a$. Similarly $f_y(a,b)=2b$. The vector formulas follow by differentiating the lifted slice parametrizations.
example: The extension of $x^3/(x^2+y^2)$ by zero has $f_x(0,0)=1$ and $f_y(0,0)=0$, obtained from the actual restrictions $f(x,0)=x$ and $f(0,y)=0$.
pitfall: Existence of both slice slopes does not imply continuity or total differentiability. Their spanning plane is only a candidate first-order approximation.
task: Move the slice $y=b$ while keeping $x=1$. Predict why the $x$-partial remains $2$ even though the height changes. Compute the corresponding $y$-partial $2b$ algebraically.
insight: Partials probe selected one-dimensional traces. Total differentiability will demand compatibility across all nearby inputs.

title: Cross products build normal vectors
subtitle: Two tangent directions determine a plane.
formula: \begin{gathered}\mathbf n=\mathbf a\times\mathbf b\\\mathbf n\cdot(\mathbf x-\mathbf p)=0\end{gathered}
definition: The cross product in oriented $\mathbb R^3$ is perpendicular to both input vectors and has magnitude $\|a\|\|b\|\sin\theta$, the area of their parallelogram. A nonzero normal and a point determine a unique plane. Two nonparallel directions instead give $p+s a+t b$.
conditions: The directions must be nonzero and nonparallel, so $a\times b\ne0$. A zero normal gives no plane equation. The sign of the cross product follows the right-hand rule.
proof: Expanding coordinates gives $a\times b=(a_2b_3-a_3b_2,a_3b_1-a_1b_3,a_1b_2-a_2b_1)$. Dotting with either input cancels term by term. For graph tangents $(1,0,f_x)$ and $(0,1,f_y)$, this gives $(-f_x,-f_y,1)$.
example: On $z=x^2+y^2$ at $(1,1,2)$, the slice directions are $(1,0,2)$ and $(0,1,2)$. Their cross product is $(-2,-2,1)$ and the plane equation becomes $z=2x+2y-2$.
pitfall: The cross product is anti-commutative and distributive, but not associative: $(\mathbf i\times\mathbf i)\times\mathbf j=0$ whereas $\mathbf i\times(\mathbf i\times\mathbf j)=-\mathbf j$.
task: Inspect the two plane directions and the normal from several camera angles. Check each dot product with the normal is zero.
insight: Parametric and normal-form descriptions encode the same plane.

title: What total differentiability means
subtitle: One affine model must become accurate faster than distance shrinks.
definition: Total differentiability means that an affine map $L$ matches $f(p)$ and has an error negligible compared with input displacement. Its linear part $Df(p)$ is the derivative. If it exists, $Df(p)h=\nabla f(p)\cdot h$ and the affine approximation is unique.
conditions: Work at an interior point. The little-$o$ condition is over all nonzero displacements approaching zero, not a few directions. The lecture calls $L$ linear or planar; in linear-algebra terminology it is affine unless its constant term vanishes.
proof: Restrict the error condition to each coordinate axis to identify the coefficients as partial derivatives. If two candidate linear parts $A,B$ worked, set $h=t v$: then $|(A-B)v|$ must be zero for every $v$, proving uniqueness. Also $f(p+h)-f(p)=Df(p)h+o(\|h\|)\to0$, so total differentiability implies continuity.
example: For $f(x,y)=x^2+y^2$ at $p=(a,b)$, $L(x,y)=a^2+b^2+2a(x-a)+2b(y-b)$. The exact remainder is $(x-a)^2+(y-b)^2$, so the normalized error equals $\|h\|$.
pitfall: A small absolute error alone is insufficient: continuity already makes errors small. Differentiability requires error divided by input distance to vanish.
task: Shrink the inspection radius. Compare the graph with its plane and watch the normalized error decrease proportionally to the radius.
insight: The tangent plane is a first-order model precisely when its residual is second-order or smaller in this quadratic example.

title: All directional derivatives can exist—and still fail
subtitle: A directional response must come from one linear map.
definition: This function is continuous at the origin and has every directional derivative there. Nevertheless it is not totally differentiable. Its candidate affine approximation, determined by the partials $(1,0)$, is $L(x,y)=x$.
conditions: The directional derivative displayed uses a unit vector $(v,w)$ and a two-sided limit in its scalar parameter. Existence of the gradient only means the coordinate partials exist; it does not authorize the gradient directional-derivative formula.
proof: Continuity follows from $|f(x,y)|\le|x|\le\sqrt{x^2+y^2}$. Substitution $(x,y)=t(v,w)$ gives $f(t v,t w)/t=v^3$. A genuine derivative with partials $(1,0)$ would give $v$, which differs at $v=1/\sqrt2$. Equivalently, along $y=x$, $|f(x,x)-x|/\sqrt{2x^2}=1/(2\sqrt2)$, never tending to zero.
example: An even stronger failure is the zero extension of $xy/(x^2+y^2)$: both partials at zero equal zero, yet the function is discontinuous because its diagonal values are $1/2$.
pitfall: Neither continuity plus partials, nor existence of every directional derivative, proves total differentiability. The directions must fit a single linear approximation with a uniform remainder bound.
task: Rotate the approach direction and compare the actual slope $\cos^3\theta$ with the candidate plane slope $\cos\theta$. Find their largest visible disagreement.
insight: Total differentiability is a compatibility and uniformity condition, not a checklist of one-dimensional derivatives.
