title: Certify the approximation
subtitle: Continuous partials and explicit remainders make the model usable.
definition: A convenient sufficient criterion is that the partial derivatives exist and are continuous throughout an open neighborhood of $p$. Then $f$ is totally differentiable at $p$. An explicit error estimate also proves differentiability directly and quantifies how far a local approximation can be trusted.
conditions: The criterion is sufficient, not necessary. More generally, existence of both partials throughout a neighborhood together with continuity of those partials at $p$ suffices. Merely knowing their values at $p$ is not enough. Measurement-error estimates from differentials are first-order estimates unless a remainder bound is included.
proof: Split $f(a+h,b+k)-f(a,b)$ into a horizontal and a vertical increment, then apply the one-variable mean-value theorem to each. The partials at the intervening points approach their values at $p$, giving $R=\varepsilon_1h+\varepsilon_2k$ with $\varepsilon_i\to0$. Conversely such a decomposition gives $|R|/\sqrt{h^2+k^2}\le\sqrt{\varepsilon_1^2+\varepsilon_2^2}$.
example: For $V(r,h)=\pi r^2h/3$ at $(10,25)$ with input errors at most $0.1$, $|dV|\le(500\pi/3)(0.1)+(100\pi/3)(0.1)=20\pi$. The exact positive error is $(\pi/3)(60.451)$, showing why $20\pi$ is an estimate rather than a rigorous upper bound.
pitfall: The supplement emphasizes neighborhood control. Do not confuse continuity of a derivative on its possibly sparse domain with its existence on an entire neighborhood.
task: Use the paraboloid to compare actual error, linear error and normalized error as the neighborhood shrinks. Identify the exact quadratic remainder.
insight: A proof of approximation should say both what tends to zero and how that quantity scales.
topics: continuity at a point versus on a neighborhood

title: The chain rule as a composition of motions
subtitle: Add the contributions through every intermediate variable.
definition: The multivariable chain rule composes linear approximations. A change in an independent variable first moves the intermediate variables; their contributions to the output then add. A dependency tree records one product of derivatives for each path and a sum over all paths to the chosen input.
conditions: The inner map must be totally differentiable at the input, the outer map totally differentiable at the resulting intermediate point, and the composition must be defined. For a curve, ordinary differentiability of its components supplies the inner derivative.
proof: Writing $g(p+h)=g(p)+Ah+o(\|h\|)$ and $f(q+k)=f(q)+Bk+o(\|k\|)$ gives $f(g(p+h))=f(g(p))+BAh+o(\|h\|)$. Coordinate multiplication of the two derivative matrices gives $\partial_i(f\circ g)=\sum_j(\partial_j f)\,\partial_i g_j$.
example: For the displayed path $\mathbf r(t)=(t,t^2)$ on $f(x,y)=x^2+y^2$, the lifted height is $t^2+t^4$. The chain rule gives $(2t,2t^2)\cdot(1,2t)=2t+4t^3$. The constant-height circle is available as a comparison; its two contributions cancel. For $g(u,v)=(u+v,u-v)$, $f\circ g=2u^2+2v^2$ has derivatives $4u,4v$.
pitfall: Evaluate the outer partials at the intermediate point $g(p)$. Having outer partials alone does not satisfy the chain-rule hypotheses.
task: Predict the sign of the output derivative before moving $t$. Compare the two partial contributions on the nonconstant path, then switch to the circle and explain the cancellation.
insight: The matrix product is the rigorous form of the dependency-tree mnemonic; it also handles longer composition chains.

title: Implicit surfaces become local graphs
subtitle: A nonzero partial derivative selects a viable coordinate chart.
definition: The implicit function theorem turns $F(x,y,z)=0$ near a suitable point into a unique local graph $z=z(x,y)$. A regular level set also has tangent plane $\nabla F(p)\cdot(X-p)=0$. In two dimensions the same statement gives a tangent line to an implicit curve.
conditions:
A safe regularity hypothesis is $F\in C^1$ on an open neighborhood of $p$, $F(p)=0$ and $F_z(p)
e0$ for a graph over the $xy$-plane. For some local coordinate graph and a regular tangent plane, require $
abla F(p)
e0$. These are local conclusions.
proof: The theorem supplies the local graph and uniqueness; this existence result is not derived here. Differentiating $F(x,y,z(x,y))=0$ by the chain rule gives $F_x+F_z z_x=0$ and $F_y+F_z z_y=0$. Differentiating any curve on the level set gives $\nabla F(p)\cdot\mathbf r'=0$, explaining its tangent directions.
example: On the unit sphere near its north pole, $z=\sqrt{1-x^2-y^2}$ and $z_x=-x/z$, $z_y=-y/z$. At an equatorial point $F_z=0$, this chart fails; at $(1,0,0)$ one can instead solve $x=\sqrt{1-y^2-z^2}$.
pitfall: A failed $F_z$ test need not mean a singular surface; another coordinate may work. Also the tangent-plane equation describes the plane, not the original curved level set.
task: Move the sphere point toward the equator. Track the vertical normal component and identify when the graph over the $xy$-plane stops being a good chart.
insight: Implicit differentiation computes derivatives of a graph whose local existence must first be justified.

title: Direction changes the slope
subtitle: Rotate the slice and measure the first-order response.
definition: A directional derivative differentiates the restriction of $f$ to the line through $p$ in a unit direction $u$. Coordinate partials are the cases $u=e_i$. The gradient is the vector of all coordinate partial derivatives.
conditions: The defining limit is meaningful independently of total differentiability. The equality to a gradient dot product requires total differentiability at the interior point. Normalize a supplied direction if the desired quantity is change per unit distance.
proof: Insert $h=t u$ into the differentiability expansion. The linear part becomes $t\nabla f(p)\cdot u$, while the error divided by $|t|=\|t u\|$ tends to zero. Dividing by $t$ therefore leaves the stated directional derivative.
example: For $f(x,y)=x^2+y^2$ at $(1,1)$, $\nabla f=(2,2)$ and $D_u f=2\cos\theta+2\sin\theta$. At direction $(2,5)$ use $u=(2,5)/\sqrt{29}$, not $(2,5)$ itself.
pitfall: A nonunit direction measures change per parameter step, which scales with the vector length. The gradient need not represent actual directional derivatives for a nondifferentiable function.
task: Rotate the unit direction and its lifted tangent. Find the two directions with zero first-order slope. Explain their relation to the level circle through $(1,1)$.
insight: At a differentiable point, every directional slope is a projection of one vector.

title: The gradient points uphill and across contours
subtitle: One vector governs both local geometry and fastest change.
definition: For a differentiable function, the gradient points in the direction of fastest first-order increase; its negative points toward fastest decrease. Along a regular level curve it is normal to the tangent. For an implicit surface $F=0$, the corresponding normal line is $p+t\nabla F(p)$.

title: Stationary does not mean optimal
subtitle: A flat first-order model can hide opposite changes.
definition: A local minimum means $f(p)\le f(x)$ for every sufficiently close allowed input; a local maximum reverses the inequality. An absolute extremum compares with the entire domain. Following the course convention, an interior critical point has either a missing partial derivative or a zero gradient. A saddle has a zero gradient and neither type of local extremum.
conditions: The necessary zero-gradient condition applies to an interior local extremum when all partials exist. Local comparisons are relative to the domain. The term stationary commonly refers only to the zero-gradient case, so distinguish it from the course broader critical-point convention.
proof: Restrict an interior local extremum to each coordinate line. The one-variable necessary condition makes every partial zero. For $a<0$, however, $f(x,0)>0$ and $f(0,y)<0$ for nonzero sufficiently small $x,y$, so zero is a saddle despite its vanishing gradient.
example: For $a>0$ the origin is the unique absolute minimum. For $a=0$, every point on the $y$-axis is a non-strict absolute minimum. For $a<0$, the origin is a saddle. A function such as $\sqrt{x^2+y^2}$ has an absolute minimum at zero with missing partials.
pitfall: Critical points are candidates, not conclusions. Boundary extrema need not have zero gradient, and a nondifferentiable extremum can be missed by solving only $\nabla f=0$.
task: Move $a$ from positive through zero to negative. Compare the signs along the two coordinate traces before naming the critical point.
insight: First derivatives locate candidates. The sign pattern of nearby changes decides whether a candidate is an extremum.

title: Second derivatives and changing slopes
subtitle: Differentiate the slope field, and track the order.
definition: Second partials differentiate first partials. Pure terms measure changes in a slope along its own coordinate; mixed terms measure how a slope changes when the other coordinate changes. Under suitable continuity hypotheses, the order of differentiation can be exchanged.
conditions: Clairaut theorem applies when both mixed partials exist and are continuous on an open neighborhood of the point. The $C^2$ hypothesis is a convenient stronger formulation. Existence of both mixed partials at a single point does not suffice.
proof: Consider the rectangular increment $f(a+h,b+k)-f(a+h,b)-f(a,b+k)+f(a,b)$. Applying the one-variable mean-value theorem first in one coordinate and then the other expresses its quotient by $hk$ as a nearby mixed partial. Reversing the order and using continuity yields the same limiting value.
example: For the displayed $f(x,y)=x^2y$, the partials are $f_x=2xy$, $f_y=x^2$, $f_{xx}=2y$, $f_{xy}=f_{yx}=2x$, $f_{yy}=0$. For the lecture example $x^2y-y^3+\log x$ on $x>0$, they become $2y-1/x^2,2x,2x,-6y$.
pitfall: Here $f_{xy}$ means differentiate first in $x$, then in $y$, so its Leibniz form is $\partial^2 f/(\partial y\,\partial x)$. Do not silently assume equality when regularity is unverified.
task: Move the slice in the transverse direction and observe its tangent slope changing. Relate that change to the mixed partial $2x$.
insight: With continuous higher partials, the order can be permuted whenever the number of differentiations in each variable is unchanged.

title: Classify the second-order shape
subtitle: The Hessian is the quadratic part left after the tangent plane.
definition: At a stationary point, the quadratic term determines the local shape when it is definite or indefinite. In two variables: $\Delta>0$ and $f_{xx}>0$ gives a strict local minimum; $\Delta>0$ and $f_{xx}<0$ gives a strict local maximum; $\Delta<0$ gives a saddle; $\Delta=0$ leaves the test inconclusive.
conditions: Require a zero gradient and continuous second partials in an open neighborhood. The Hessian is then symmetric. When the quadratic form is degenerate, higher-order terms or direct inequalities must decide the behavior.
proof: The second-order expansion is $f(p+h)-f(p)=\tfrac12h^TH_f(p)h+o(\|h\|^2)$. A positive definite quadratic form has a positive lower bound proportional to $\|h\|^2$, dominating the remainder; negative definiteness reverses signs. An indefinite form has positive and negative directions, giving a saddle.
example: For $x^2+a y^2$, $H=\operatorname{diag}(2,2a)$ and $\Delta=4a$. At $a=0$ the test is inconclusive even though direct inspection gives a minimum. More generally $x^4+y^4$ has a minimum and $x^4-y^4$ a saddle at zero, both with zero Hessian. For $\sin(xy)$, zero is a saddle; the critical hyperbolas $xy=(k+1/2)\pi$ are global maxima for even $k$ and minima for odd $k$, despite $\Delta=0$ there.
pitfall: Inconclusive means the theorem gives no classification. It does not mean no extremum exists. A local test also does not establish a global optimum.
task: Change $a$ and match the two principal curvatures with the determinant sign. At zero, classify the surface directly after the test falls silent.
insight: The determinant detects whether the two principal quadratic directions agree in sign or oppose each other.

title: Global extrema require the boundary
subtitle: Existence first; then compare every candidate value.
definition: The extreme value theorem guarantees a minimum and maximum for a continuous real function on a nonempty compact domain. In Euclidean space, compact means closed and bounded. To find the extrema, inspect interior critical points and optimize every boundary component, including corners, then compare their values.
conditions: Continuity and a nonempty closed bounded domain guarantee attainment. If these hypotheses fail, extrema may still exist but are not guaranteed. Do not apply a local second-derivative classification as a substitute for comparing global candidate values.
proof: For the displayed rectangle, the interior equations $2x-2y=0$ and $-2x+2=0$ give $(1,1)$ with value one. Boundary restrictions are $x^2$, $9-4y$, $(x-2)^2$ and $2y$. Their one-variable extrema yield absolute minimum zero at $(0,0)$ and $(2,2)$, and absolute maximum nine at $(3,0)$.
example: The set $\mathbb Q\cap[0,1]$ is bounded but not closed in $\mathbb R$, since it omits irrational limit points. On $\mathbb R^2$, the function $x^2-xy+y^2-2x+y=(x-1-y/2)^2+3y^2/4-1$ still has minimum $-1$ at $(1,0)$, but no maximum.
pitfall: Checking only the interior stationary point misses both global extrema in this example. A bounded domain need not be closed, and a bounded function need not attain its supremum.
task: Follow each of the four boundary traces. Collect its smallest and largest heights, then compare with the interior critical value.
insight: Existence is a theorem about the domain and continuity. Identification is a complete comparison over the interior and boundary.

title: Lagrange multipliers on a curve
subtitle: An extremum has no first-order motion along the constraint.
definition: To optimize $f$ subject to $g=k$, restrict the domain of $f$ to that level set. At a regular constrained local extremum, the gradient of $f$ belongs to the normal line of the constraint. The multiplier $\lambda$ records the proportionality of the two gradients; it is an auxiliary unknown, not the value being optimized.
conditions: Assume $f,g$ are $C^1$ on an open neighbourhood of $p$, $g(p)=k$, and $\nabla g(p)\ne0$. The multiplier equation is necessary for a local extremum. Global existence follows if the entire feasible set is nonempty and compact and $f$ is continuous. Include any singular constraint points separately.
proof: By the implicit function theorem, the regular level set is locally a smooth curve. Every tangent vector $v$ satisfies $\nabla g(p)\cdot v=0$. Differentiating $f$ along feasible curves through a local extremum gives $\nabla f(p)\cdot v=0$. In the plane, vectors perpendicular to the same nonzero tangent form a one-dimensional space, hence the multiplier equation.
example: The scene uses $f=x+y$ and $g=x^2+y^2=1$. Its feasible point is $(\cos t,\sin t)$ and its height is $\cos t+\sin t$. Solving $(1,1)=2\lambda(x,y)$ yields extrema $\pm\sqrt2$, attained at $(\pm1/\sqrt2,\pm1/\sqrt2)$ with matching signs.
pitfall: A multiplier solution is a candidate, not automatically a maximum. Dividing by $x$, $y$, or $\lambda$ can discard candidates when those quantities vanish. Tangency seen in a mesh cannot establish the theorem.
task: Move the point to the greatest and least heights. Explain why the height derivative $-\sin t+\cos t$ vanishes at each, although the unconstrained gradient $(1,1)$ never vanishes.
insight: Constrained stationarity concerns feasible directions. A nonzero gradient can be normal to every allowed motion.

title: One constraint in three dimensions
subtitle: The constraint is a surface; its normal still has one dimension.
definition: For one regular scalar constraint in $\mathbb R^3$, allowable first-order displacements lie in the tangent plane $\ker Dg(p)$. A constrained extremum forces $Df(p)$ to vanish on that plane, so $\nabla f(p)$ is parallel to its normal $\nabla g(p)$. The graph of a three-variable objective would require four dimensions; the scene therefore shows its constraint in physical space.
conditions: Use $C^1$ functions on an open set and require $\nabla g(p)\ne0$. The theorem locates existing extrema. A closed and bounded feasible set with continuous objective guarantees both global extrema; otherwise establish global bounds or limiting behaviour separately.
proof:
The regular level-set theorem identifies the tangent plane with $\{v:
abla g(p)\cdot v=0\}$. Differentiation along every feasible curve gives $
abla f(p)\cdot v=0$ on this plane. Its orthogonal complement is the span of $
abla g(p)$, which proves the equation.
example: On the unit sphere, take $f=x+y+z$. Cauchy–Schwarz gives $|f|\le\sqrt3\sqrt{x^2+y^2+z^2}=\sqrt3$. Equality occurs precisely at $p=\pm(1,1,1)/\sqrt3$. Thus the candidate comparison is certified by a global inequality.
pitfall: On a noncompact constraint, comparing stationary values alone does not settle the global problem. For the lecture’s open-top box, $xy+2xz+2yz=12$ with positive dimensions, AM–GM gives $(xy)(2xz)(2yz)\le4^3$, hence $xyz\le4$; equality gives $(x,y,z)=(2,2,1)$.
task: Locate the sphere point in the direction $(1,1,1)$. Explain why moving in any tangent direction gives zero first-order change there, and use Cauchy–Schwarz to certify that it is the global maximum.
insight: The dimensional change affects the feasible tangent space, while the one-constraint normal equation stays the same.

title: Two constraints and one tangent direction
subtitle: The objective gradient belongs to the span of two independent normals.
definition: Two independent regular constraints in $\mathbb R^3$ locally intersect in a curve. Its tangent direction is parallel to $\nabla g\times\nabla h$. At a constrained extremum, the objective has zero derivative along that curve, so its gradient lies in the plane spanned by the two constraint gradients.
conditions: Assume $f,g,h$ are $C^1$ near the feasible point and require $\nabla g$ and $\nabla h$ to be linearly independent there. Merely requiring both gradients to be nonzero is insufficient. Test points where their cross product vanishes separately.
proof: The rank-two implicit function theorem makes the feasible tangent space $\ker D(g,h)(p)$. Its orthogonal complement is the row space of $D(g,h)(p)$, namely $\operatorname{span}\{\nabla g(p),\nabla h(p)\}$. Stationarity says $Df(p)$ annihilates the tangent space, which produces the two multipliers.
example: The scene intersects $g=x^2+y^2+z^2=1$ with $h=z=0$. For $f=x+y$, solving $(1,1,0)=\lambda(2x,2y,2z)+\mu(0,0,1)$ gives $z=0$, $\mu=0$, and the two extrema $\pm\sqrt2$ on the equatorial circle.
pitfall: Nonzero constraint normals alone are insufficient; they must be independent for this theorem. For $g=x$ and $h=x+y^2$, the feasible line $x=y=0$ makes $f=y$ constant, but its gradient is outside the span of the two equal constraint gradients.
task: Identify the two surface normals at a point of the intersection. At a maximizing point, verify that the objective gradient has no component along their cross product.
insight: The number of independent constraints determines the dimension of the normal span, not merely the number of equations written down.

title: A double integral from columns
subtitle: Refine the mesh and distinguish convergence from a persuasive picture.
definition: Divide a closed axis-parallel rectangle into subrectangles and choose an arbitrary sample point in each. Multiply each sampled height by its base area and sum. The double Riemann integral exists when these sums approach the same finite value for every choice of sample points as the maximum subrectangle diameter tends to zero. For nonnegative $f$, this gives the volume beneath the graph.
conditions: Continuity on a closed rectangle is a sufficient condition for integrability. The definition demands one common limit for all samplings; convergence of the displayed midpoint sums alone is weaker. When $f$ can be negative, the integral is signed accumulation; geometric volume uses $|f|$.
proof: A continuous function on a compact rectangle is uniformly continuous. The oscillation of $f$ in each cell therefore tends uniformly to zero with the mesh size. The difference between upper and lower sums is bounded by the total area times the largest cell oscillation, hence tends to zero. Every sampled sum is trapped between them.
example: The displayed surface is $f(x,y)=3-(x^2+y^2)/2$ on $[-1,1]^2$. Its exact volume is $32/3$. With $n$ equal subdivisions in each direction, the midpoint sum is $32/3+4/(3n^2)$, so this particular approximation decreases to the integral from above.
pitfall: A finite collection of rectangular columns is an approximation, with flat tops that do not reproduce the surface. The sign of approximation error depends on the function and sampling; midpoint sums do not always overestimate.
task: Increase the subdivision count. Compare the remaining gaps and overlaps with the formula $4/(3n^2)$ for this example’s midpoint error.
insight: The integral is independent of sampling because local variation becomes uniformly small, not because one animation appears to settle.

title: Integrating a bounded region
subtitle: Zero extension turns an arbitrary region into a rectangular problem.
definition: For bounded $D\subset R$, define $\iint_D f\,dA$ as the Riemann integral on the closed rectangle $R$ of the zero extension $\widetilde f=f$ on $D$ and $0$ on $R\setminus D$, provided that integral exists. Enlarging $R$ adds only zero-valued cells, so the value is independent of the containing rectangle. The area of $D$ is the integral of its indicator when that integral exists.
conditions: The precise existence test used here is the Lebesgue criterion for Riemann integrability: a bounded function on a closed rectangle is Riemann integrable exactly when its discontinuity set has Lebesgue measure zero. In particular, if $D$ is compact with Jordan-null boundary and $f$ is continuous on $D$, then $\widetilde f$ is bounded and any discontinuity lies on the boundary. Continuity on a nonclosed bounded $D$ alone need not give boundedness.
proof: First establish rectangle integrability of $\widetilde f$ by the stated criterion. If $R\subset R'$ both contain $D$, the extension on $R'\setminus R$ is zero; additivity for rectangles gives the same integral. The boundary condition is an existence argument, not an application of continuous-rectangle Fubini to a discontinuous extension.
example: For the displayed triangle $D=\{x,y\ge0:x+y\le2\}$, $\operatorname{Area}(D)=2$. The scene’s density $f=1+x+y$ has mass $14/3$. Extending $q=(3/14)(1+x+y)$ by zero outside $D$ gives a joint probability density on $\mathbb R^2$; integrating $q$ over a subregion gives its probability.
pitfall: A bounded set need not have Jordan area. For the rational-coordinate points in $[0,1]^2$, the zero extension of $1$ is discontinuous everywhere and has no Riemann integral, although that set has Lebesgue measure zero. These frameworks answer different questions.
task: Read the triangle as the support of a density. Explain why the density is zero outside it and why changing finitely many boundary values does not alter total mass.
insight: The same integral describes volume, mass, or probability according to the meaning and units of its integrand.

title: Fubini: accumulate one direction at a time
subtitle: One volume admits two families of slices.
definition: An iterated integral first holds one coordinate fixed and integrates over the other. Its inner integral is then a function of the remaining coordinate. Fubini’s theorem identifies both orders of iteration with the double integral under suitable hypotheses.
conditions: The course theorem stated here requires $f$ continuous on the entire closed rectangle $[a,b]\times[c,d]$. Then both inner integrals exist for every outer coordinate and both orders equal the rectangle integral. A zero extension over a nonrectangular region can jump at its boundary, so its use requires a separate region-slicing theorem or stronger Fubini hypotheses.
proof: For continuous $f$, uniform continuity controls the approximation error uniformly across every slice. Finite double sums may be grouped by rows or by columns without changing their sum. Taking the uniformly controlled limits in these two groupings gives the two iterated integrals.
example: For $f=3-(x^2+y^2)/2$ on $[-1,1]^2$, integrating first in $y$ gives the slice area $A(x)=17/3-x^2$. Then $\int_{-1}^{1}A(x)\,dx=32/3$. Swapping $x$ and $y$ gives the same calculation because this example is symmetric.
pitfall: Continuity of $f$ only on a triangular region does not make its zero extension continuous on the enclosing rectangle. The continuous-rectangle Fubini theorem therefore cannot, by itself, justify the triangular slice formula. Derive the region bounds and invoke its slicing theorem.
task: View the columns in rows parallel to each coordinate axis. Interpret a row’s limiting sum as a slice area and its outer accumulation as the full volume.
insight: Integration order changes how the same accumulation is organized; it does not change the region being measured.

title: Type I and Type II regions
subtitle: Bounds are a geometric description, read from the inside outward.
definition: A Type I planar region has one vertical interval over each $x\in[a,b]$: $g_1(x)\le y\le g_2(x)$. A Type II region has one horizontal interval over each $y\in[c,d]$: $h_1(y)\le x\le h_2(y)$. A region may admit both descriptions. The displayed equality applies when both sets of bounds describe exactly the same region.
conditions: Assume continuous bounding functions with lower bound no greater than upper bound and a continuous integrand on the resulting closed region. These hypotheses give existence of the integral and the slicing formula. If a vertical or horizontal line meets multiple disjoint intervals, split the region or choose a different description.
proof: The continuous ordered boundary functions make the compact Type I or II region Jordan measurable; the continuous integrand has a Riemann-integrable zero extension. A region-slicing theorem, proved from rectangular upper/lower sums or by an applicable stronger Fubini result, then identifies the integral with the inner section integral. This is not a direct application of the continuity-only rectangle Fubini theorem, because the zero extension may jump at the boundary. Reversal requires new bounds describing the identical set.
example: The triangle is $0\le x\le2$, $0\le y\le2-x$, and also $0\le y\le2$, $0\le x\le2-y$. For $f=1+x+y$, the first inner integral is $4-x-x^2/2$, so the volume is $14/3$. Both descriptions include the entire triangle once.
pitfall: For a square frame with a central square removed, middle vertical and horizontal slices each have two disjoint intervals. The frame is neither Type I nor Type II as one piece; split it into rectangles with only boundary overlap before using slice formulas. Merely exchanging $dx$ and $dy$ leaves incorrect bounds.
task: Move the slice across the triangle. At each position, identify its two endpoints from the inequalities before evaluating the inner integral.
insight: Every integration limit has a geometric job: it specifies where a slice starts, where it stops, or how the slices sweep the region.

title: Linearity and cutting a region
subtitle: Add functions algebraically; add regions geometrically.
definition: Linearity concerns addition and scaling of integrands on one region. Domain additivity concerns decomposing a region into finitely many pieces. Restricting a function to a smaller region simply uses its original values there. These operations allow complicated regions to be assembled from Type I or Type II pieces.
conditions: For linearity, both functions must be integrable on the same region. For finite region additivity, each restricted integral must exist and pairwise overlaps must have Jordan area zero. Piecewise smooth shared boundaries qualify; overlapping interiors do not. Use the zero-extension definition on a common containing rectangle.
proof: Finite Riemann sums are linear and their limits preserve linearity. For a finite union of Jordan regions with Jordan-null overlaps, their indicators add except on null overlaps. Multiplication by the bounded integrand and Riemann integrability make those overlap contributions zero; additivity follows. The result does not authorize arbitrary pathological pieces.
example: Split the displayed triangle at $x=1$. For $f=1+x+y$, the left integral is $\int_0^1(4-x-x^2/2)\,dx=10/3$ and the right integral is $\int_1^2(4-x-x^2/2)\,dx=4/3$. Their sum is $14/3$; the shared segment contributes zero area.
pitfall: Additivity does not permit overlapping pieces of positive area without correction. Integrability over the whole domain also does not automatically give integrability on an arbitrary pathological subset.
task: Place the slice at $x=1$ and identify the two pieces. Explain why including the cut in both pieces does not change the answer.
insight: A good decomposition simplifies bounds while preserving an exact accounting of every part of the region.

title: Polar coordinates and the area factor
subtitle: Equal angular steps become wider farther from the origin.
definition: A polar coordinate pair records nonnegative radius $r$ and angle $\theta$. The image of $[a,b]\times[\alpha,\beta]$ is a polar rectangle: usually an annular sector, not a Cartesian rectangle. The same Cartesian point can have many angle representatives; the origin has no unique angle.
conditions: Take $0\le a\le b$ and $0\le\beta-\alpha\le2\pi$ to avoid covering positive-area portions repeatedly. A continuous integrand on the resulting compact sector can be integrated as $\int_\alpha^\beta\int_a^b f(r\cos\theta,r\sin\theta)r\,dr\,d\theta$.
proof: An annular cell from $r_-$ to $r_+$ with angular width $\Delta\theta$ has exact area $(r_+^2-r_-^2)\Delta\theta/2=r_*\Delta r\Delta\theta$, where $r_*=(r_-+r_+)/2$. Thus polar Riemann sums acquire the factor $r$. In the infinitesimal description, radial and angular edge lengths are $dr$ and $r\,d\theta$.
example: The scene has outer radius $2$ and angular sweep $\beta$ from $0$. Its area is $\int_0^\beta\int_0^2r\,dr\,d\theta=2\beta$. A quarter disk has $\beta=\pi/2$ and area $\pi$; the full disk has area $4\pi$.
pitfall: Angles in these formulas are radians. Replacing $dA$ by $dr\,d\theta$ gives the area of a parameter rectangle, not the area of its Cartesian image.
task: Increase the sector angle. Compare an equal angular interval near the origin and near the outer circle, and explain the larger area of the outer cells.
insight: The factor $r$ corrects the local distortion created by the coordinate map.

title: Variable polar bounds
subtitle: Describe the region by the intervals a ray crosses.
definition: A polar region consists of points whose angle lies in an interval and whose radius lies between two functions of that angle. For each fixed $\theta$, the ray meets the region in one radial interval. Polar rectangles are the special case with constant radial bounds.
conditions: Assume continuous functions $0\le h_1\le h_2$ and a continuous integrand on the compact image. Keep the angle span at most $2\pi$. For a full revolution the course assumes the radial boundaries match at its ends. More complicated regions can be split into finitely many suitable pieces.
proof: The parameter domain is a Type II planar region in coordinates $(r,\theta)$. Apply the polar area factor $r$, then integrate over its radial intervals. For $f=1$, integrating in $r$ gives the area formula $\frac12\int_\alpha^\beta(h_2^2-h_1^2)\,d\theta$.
example: The displayed disk is $(x-1)^2+y^2\le1$. Substitution gives $r^2-2r\cos\theta\le0$. Off the origin, the bounds are $-\pi/2\le\theta\le\pi/2$ and $0<r\le2\cos\theta$. Include $r=0$ separately. Its area is $\int_{-\pi/2}^{\pi/2}2\cos^2\theta\,d\theta=\pi$.
pitfall: The current scene displays the shifted disk and its variable radial interval. Do not replace the bound $2\cos\theta$ with a constant radius. When dividing $r^2\le2r\cos\theta$ by $r$, handle $r=0$ separately and require a nonnegative upper radial bound.
task: Predict where the radial interval is longest, then sweep the ray across the disk. Derive its upper bound and explain why the endpoint angles leave only the origin.
insight: Choose coordinates that make intersections with coordinate lines simple; the resulting bounds become a readable description of the geometry.

title: A triple integral accumulates through space
subtitle: Integrating 1 measures a solid; integrating density measures its mass.
definition: Partition a closed axis-parallel box into small boxes, sample $f$ in each, multiply by the cell volume, and sum. A triple Riemann integral requires a common finite limit for every sampling as every subdivision grows. For a general bounded solid, extend the function by zero to an enclosing box.
conditions: Continuity on a closed box ensures integrability and equality with all six iterated orders. For a bounded region with volume, a bounded continuous density suffices. A bounded region has Jordan volume precisely when its boundary has zero Jordan volume. A continuous graph over a compact planar domain has zero three-dimensional volume, even if its surface area is positive.
proof: Uniform continuity makes upper and lower box sums converge together. A zero-volume boundary contributes arbitrarily little for bounded integrands, so zero extension defines the integral independently of the chosen enclosing box. Grouping finite sums in the six possible coordinate orders and passing through the controlled limits gives Fubini’s theorem.
example: The scene’s solid is $E=\{x^2+y^2\le2,\ 0\le z\le2-x^2-y^2\}$. At height $z$, its horizontal section is a disk of radius $\sqrt{2-z}$ and area $\pi(2-z)$. Thus $\operatorname{Vol}(E)=\int_0^2\pi(2-z)\,dz=2\pi$.
pitfall: The displayed solid is the domain of integration. The graph of a scalar function of three variables would lie in four dimensions, so its integral should not be described as the usual three-dimensional volume under that graph.
task: Move the horizontal slice upward. Derive its radius from the solid’s inequality and explain why adding slice area times thickness gives the volume.
insight: The dimension of the integration element is the dimension of the domain: area for double integrals, volume for triple integrals.

title: Type I, II and III solids
subtitle: Choose the coordinate whose fibres are single intervals.
definition: A Type I solid has $z$ between two functions of $(x,y)$. Type II has $x$ between functions of $(y,z)$, and Type III has $y$ between functions of $(x,z)$. The remaining two coordinates describe the projection. A solid can have several such descriptions.
conditions: Use a compact planar projection with area, continuous lower and upper bounds, and continuous $f$ on the resulting solid. Requiring the projection to have area avoids pathological compact sets. If fibres have gaps, split the domain into finitely many simple solids.
proof: For a fixed projected point, the zero extension is nonzero on exactly the interval between the two boundary functions. Integrating along that fibre removes one coordinate. Fubini then accumulates the resulting function over the projection. Repeating this in a different direction changes the bounds but not the solid.
example: For the displayed solid, Type I bounds are $x^2+y^2\le2$, $0\le z\le2-x^2-y^2$. Type II bounds use $0\le z\le2$, $|y|\le\sqrt{2-z}$, and $-\sqrt{2-z-y^2}\le x\le\sqrt{2-z-y^2}$. Type III follows by swapping $x$ and $y$.
pitfall: Project the entire solid, not just one convenient boundary. All inner bounds must be meaningful throughout the outer domain; a negative square-root argument usually exposes inconsistent bounds.
task: At a chosen height, trace the circular section. For a fixed $y$ in that section, identify the left and right $x$ endpoints and recover the Type II bounds.
insight: A triple integral is a nested set of geometric decisions: choose a projection, choose a fibre, then determine its endpoints.

title: Cylindrical coordinates
subtitle: Separate distance from the axis, angle around it, and height.
definition: Cylindrical coordinates combine planar polar coordinates with the ordinary height $z$. A constant positive $r$ is a circular cylinder, constant $\theta$ is a vertical half-plane, and constant $z$ is a horizontal plane. The angle is the azimuth measured in the $xy$-plane from the positive $x$-axis.
conditions: Take $r\ge0$ and choose one interval of length $2\pi$ for the azimuth when uniqueness is required. The angle is undefined geometrically on the $z$-axis; its multiple parameter representations do not alter the points themselves. The inverse angle must distinguish quadrants.
proof: The equations $x=r\cos\theta$ and $y=r\sin\theta$ come from the planar right triangle. Squaring and adding gives $x^2+y^2=r^2$, while $z$ remains unchanged. Thus $r=c$ is a cylinder and $|z|=r$ becomes the double cone $z^2=x^2+y^2$.
example: The scene’s cylinder is $0\le r\le1$, $0\le z\le2$. Its highlighted wedge selects an azimuthal interval $0\le\theta\le\beta$. The points $(1,0,1)$ and $(0,1,1)$ have the same radial distance and height but azimuths differing by $\pi/2$.
pitfall: $r$ is distance to the $z$-axis, not distance to the origin. Using $\arctan(y/x)$ without quadrant information can select the wrong point.
task: Rotate the wedge and identify which coordinate changes. Compare a point on the top rim with the point immediately below it on the bottom rim.
insight: Coordinates are descriptions of points; their constant-coordinate surfaces explain which shapes they simplify.

title: Cylindrical volume elements
subtitle: A thin wedge has two straight dimensions and one angular dimension.
definition: In cylindrical coordinates, a small box in parameter space becomes a curved wedge in physical space. Its local side lengths are $dr$, $r\,d\theta$, and $dz$, so its volume element is $r\,dr\,d\theta\,dz$. This is especially useful when the solid projects to a polar region.
conditions: Describe the solid with continuous radial and height bounds that cover it once apart from boundary sets of zero volume. A continuous integrand on the compact solid is sufficient. Transform both the integrand and every boundary equation; retain the factor $r$ even when the integrand itself is already radial.
proof: First integrate along vertical fibres in Cartesian coordinates. Then convert the outer planar double integral to polar coordinates, which contributes $r$. This derives the cylindrical formula directly from the already established Type I solid and polar formulas.
example: For the displayed wedge $0\le r\le1$, $0\le z\le2$, $0\le\theta\le\beta$, volume is $\int_0^\beta\int_0^1\int_0^2r\,dz\,dr\,d\theta=\beta$. The full cylinder has volume $2\pi$. If its density is $r$, mass is $\int_0^{2\pi}\int_0^1\int_0^2r^2\,dz\,dr\,d\theta=4\pi/3$.
pitfall: If density is $\sqrt{x^2+y^2}$, it becomes $r$ and the transformed integrand is $r^2$ after including the volume factor. These two occurrences of $r$ have different roles.
task: Set the angular wedge to half a revolution. Predict its volume before checking the integral, then explain why radial density changes mass without changing the shape.
insight: The Jacobian belongs to the coordinate geometry; the density belongs to the quantity being accumulated.

title: Spherical coordinates
subtitle: Distance from the origin, azimuth, and inclination play different roles.
definition: Here $\rho$ is distance from the origin, $\theta$ is azimuth in the $xy$-plane, and $\phi$ is inclination from the positive $z$-axis. This convention gives $r=\rho\sin\phi$ and $z=\rho\cos\phi$. A sphere has constant $\rho$; fixed azimuth gives a vertical half-plane.
conditions: Use $\rho\ge0$, $0\le\phi\le\pi$, and an azimuth interval of length $2\pi$. At the poles azimuth is not unique, and at the origin neither angle identifies a unique direction. Coordinate conventions vary between books, so always inspect their definitions.
proof: Decompose the radius vector into its vertical component $\rho\cos\phi$ and horizontal length $\rho\sin\phi$, then apply planar polar coordinates to that horizontal component. Squaring the three components gives $x^2+y^2+z^2=\rho^2$.
example: The scene’s sphere has radius $2$. The boundary of the polar cap at inclination $\phi=\alpha$ is the circle $z=2\cos\alpha$ of radius $2\sin\alpha$. At $\alpha=\pi/2$ it is the equator. For fixed $0<\phi<\pi$, the coordinate surface is a cone except at $\phi=\pi/2$, where it is the plane $z=0$.
pitfall: Inclination is measured from the vertical axis, not from the horizontal plane. The cap shown on the sphere is a surface patch; its interior solid is a different object requiring a radial interval.
task: Move the cap boundary from the north pole toward the equator. Predict its height and radius from $2\cos\alpha$ and $2\sin\alpha$.
insight: Constant-coordinate surfaces let you translate geometric boundaries into equations before attempting an integral.

title: Spherical wedges and radial bounds
subtitle: Angular cells shrink near the poles and grow quadratically with radius.
definition: A spherical wedge is the image of intervals in radius, azimuth and inclination. Its local edge lengths are $d\rho$, $\rho\,d\phi$, and $\rho\sin\phi\,d\theta$. Multiplying them gives the spherical volume factor. Type II spherical regions allow radial bounds $g_1(\theta,\phi)\le\rho\le g_2(\theta,\phi)$.
conditions: Use nonnegative continuous radial bounds, $0\le\phi\le\pi$, and at most one azimuthal revolution, with a continuous integrand on the compact solid. Standard polar and seam singularities lie on zero-volume sets and do not change the integral. Match periodic boundary functions for a full revolution.
proof: The spherical derivative columns are mutually orthogonal away from the coordinate singularities. Their lengths are $1$, $\rho\sin\phi$, and $\rho$, so the absolute determinant is $\rho^2\sin\phi$. The change-of-variables theorem then supplies the formula; the little-edge calculation explains its geometry.
example: The solid sector beneath the displayed cap is $0\le\rho\le2$, $0\le\theta\le2\pi$, $0\le\phi\le\alpha$. Its volume is $(16\pi/3)(1-\cos\alpha)$. At $\alpha=\pi$ this is the ball volume $32\pi/3$. The curved cap alone has area $8\pi(1-\cos\alpha)$, a different quantity.
pitfall: A spherical sector extends to the origin; a solid cap cut off by a horizontal plane generally does not. A sphere such as $x^2+y^2+z^2=z$ gives the variable radial bound $0\le\rho\le\cos\phi$ where $\cos\phi\ge0$, not a constant radius about the origin.
task: Use the visible cap to identify an inclination interval. State separately the radial interval needed to turn those directions into a solid and explain the factor $\sin\phi$ near a pole.
insight: Spherical bounds describe directions and distances along those directions; they need not describe a sphere centred at the origin.

title: A determinant scales area
subtitle: A unit square becomes a parallelogram with an exact area ratio.
definition: A plane transformation maps parameter points $(u,v)$ to physical points $(x,y)$. A linear map is determined by its images of the coordinate basis vectors; these become the edges of the image of the unit square. The absolute determinant measures area scaling and its sign records orientation.
conditions: For an invertible linear map and a bounded region with area, the image has area $|\det T|$ times the original area. With bounded continuous integrands, the transformed integral includes both composition with $T$ and this constant area factor. A singular linear map collapses the plane to lower dimension.
proof: If the image edge vectors are $a=(a_1,a_2)$ and $b=(b_1,b_2)$, the parallelogram area is $|a_1b_2-a_2b_1|$. Scaling source edges by $\Delta u$ and $\Delta v$ scales that area by $\Delta u\Delta v$. Partitioning a region into small rectangles and passing to the integral proves the area formula.
example: The scene deforms the unit square using $T_s(u,v)=((1+s)u+sv,su+(1+s)v)$. Its determinant is $1+2s$. At $s=1$, the vertices are $(0,0),(2,1),(3,3),(1,2)$ and the area is $3$.
pitfall: The determinant changes during the interpolation: it is $3$ only at the completed map. A negative determinant would reverse orientation while leaving physical area positive through the absolute value.
task: Compare the image of the horizontal and vertical unit vectors. At the end of the deformation, compute their determinant and check it against the area ratio.
insight: The determinant describes what happens to small regions, not just to individual points.

title: The Jacobian is a local determinant
subtitle: A nonlinear map is approximately linear at each regular point.
definition: For $T=(X,Y)$, the derivative matrix contains the partial derivatives of each output with respect to each input. Its columns describe how the two coordinate directions move. The scalar Jacobian is the determinant of that matrix; its absolute value is the local area scaling factor.
conditions: Differentiability gives the local linear approximation. A $C^1$ map with nonzero Jacobian near a point has a local $C^1$ inverse by the inverse function theorem. This is a local statement and does not ensure one-to-one behaviour across a whole region.
proof: Differentiability means $T(p+h)=T(p)+DT(p)h+o(\|h\|)$. Thus very small parameter cells approach the shape produced by the linear map $DT(p)$. For a regular map, the ratio of their image area to source area tends to $|\det DT(p)|$. The full integral theorem makes this limiting argument precise.
example: The displayed nonlinear map is $T(u,v)=(u,(1+u)v)$. Its derivative is $\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\v&1+u\end{pmatrix}$ and its determinant is $1+u$. The unit square becomes a trapezoid of area $3/2$. The linear comparison remains available in the experiment selector.
pitfall: The Jacobian matrix and its determinant are related but different objects. A nonzero determinant rules out local collapse; it does not prevent two far-apart parameter points from mapping to the same output.
task: Predict which side of the parameter square expands more. Move the cell, then select Shrink the cell and compare the finite area ratio with the derivative determinant.
insight: Nonlinear change of variables is linear algebra applied locally, with the determinant allowed to vary from point to point.

title: Space transformations and signed Jacobians
subtitle: Volume uses the absolute determinant; coordinate order controls its sign.
definition: A space transformation $T=(X,Y,Z)$ maps three parameter coordinates to three physical coordinates. Its derivative sends a small parameter box to a parallelepiped. The determinant is a signed volume ratio, while its absolute value is the factor in an ordinary triple integral.
conditions: Keep an explicit order for the input coordinates. The course uses $(\rho,\theta,\phi)$, with $\phi$ the inclination; in this order the spherical determinant is negative away from singularities. Ordinary volume on $\rho\ge0$, $0\le\phi\le\pi$ uses $\rho^2\sin\phi$.
proof: The three derivative columns give the edges of the local parallelepiped, whose signed volume is their scalar triple product. For the spherical map ordered $(\rho,\theta,\phi)$, evaluating at $\theta=0$, $\phi=\pi/2$ gives columns $(1,0,0)$, $(0,\rho,0)$, $(0,0,-\rho)$ and sign negative. The full determinant is $-\rho^2\sin\phi$.
example: For cylindrical coordinates in the order $(r,\theta,z)$, the derivative is block triangular and has determinant $r$. For spherical coordinates, swapping the input order to $(\rho,\phi,\theta)$ swaps two columns and changes the determinant to $+\rho^2\sin\phi$, without changing the volume factor.
pitfall: Calling $\rho^2\sin\phi$ “the Jacobian” sometimes means its absolute value. Distinguish that convention from the signed determinant, especially when checking a calculation or changing variable order.
task: Locate the equator on the sphere. Identify the directions of increasing radius, azimuth and inclination, and determine their orientation using the scalar triple product.
insight: Orientation is algebraic information; geometric volume remains nonnegative.

title: Change of variables in two and three dimensions
subtitle: Transform the region, the function and the measure together.
definition: The change-of-variables theorem replaces integration over a complicated physical region with integration over a simpler parameter region. The new integrand evaluates the old function at the mapped point and multiplies by the local area or volume distortion. The notation above denotes a double or triple integral according to the dimension.
conditions: A clean sufficient version assumes $D$ is compact with Jordan area or volume, $T$ is a $C^1$ diffeomorphism on an open neighbourhood of $D$, and $f$ is continuous on $T(D)$. Standard polar, cylindrical and spherical formulas also allow their familiar zero-measure boundary seams and singularities, while requiring injectivity on the relevant interior.
proof: Partition parameter space finely. On each small cell, the map is close to its derivative, the integral contribution is close to $f(T(u))$ times the cell’s image measure, and that measure is approximated by $|\det DT(u)|$ times the source measure. Uniform control and injectivity prevent local approximation errors and double counting from surviving the limit.
example: For the displayed $T(u,v)=(u,(1+u)v)$ on $[0,1]^2$, the image is $0\le x\le1$, $0\le y\le1+x$. The Jacobian factor is $1+u$. Thus area is $3/2$, while $\iint_R y\,dA=\int_0^1\int_0^1(1+u)^2v\,dv\,du=7/6$.
pitfall: Changing only the variables inside $f$ is incomplete: the bounds and the measure must also change. If a map covers a positive-area region twice, the simple formula counts it twice unless the domain is restricted or multiplicity is handled.
task: Translate all four sides of the parameter square into the trapezoid boundary. Identify the transformed field, area factor and parameter bounds before calculating.
insight: A successful substitution is an exact correspondence between regions, equipped with the correct local scaling.

title: When the substitution is given backwards
subtitle: Compute the inverse determinant at corresponding points.
definition: A problem often suggests new coordinates $u=U(x,y)$ and $v=V(x,y)$, which specify the inverse map. You may solve for $x,y$ explicitly, or compute the inverse Jacobian and rewrite $f/|J_{T^{-1}}|$ entirely in the new variables. Boundary equations often become constant-coordinate lines.
conditions: Both maps must be differentiable inverse maps on the relevant regular region, so the determinant is nonzero. The reciprocal relationship compares corresponding points: the inverse Jacobian at $(x,y)$ corresponds to the forward Jacobian at $(u,v)=T^{-1}(x,y)$.
proof: Differentiate $T^{-1}\circ T=\mathrm{id}$ using the chain rule. This gives $D(T^{-1})(T(u))DT(u)=I$. Taking determinants gives the reciprocal identity. Substituting it into the forward change-of-variables formula yields the inverse-Jacobian method.
example: For the displayed final map, $u=(2x-y)/3$ and $v=(-x+2y)/3$. Thus $J_{T^{-1}}=1/3$. Its parallelogram is described by $0\le2x-y\le3$ and $0\le-x+2y\le3$, which become $0\le u,v\le1$. Dividing by $|1/3|$ supplies the forward area factor $3$.
pitfall: Do not multiply by the inverse determinant when transforming from $(x,y)$ to parameter integration in $(u,v)$; use its reciprocal. Absolute values are still required for ordinary area and volume.
task: Use the four slanted boundary lines to recover the square’s four constant-coordinate bounds. Verify the reciprocal determinants directly.
insight: The direction of the substitution determines which derivative appears, but the chain rule keeps the two descriptions consistent.

title: A scalar field along a curve
subtitle: Height times small arc length gives a ribbon contribution.
definition: A scalar line integral sums a scalar value along a curve, weighted by arc length. For a nonnegative function on a planar curve, it can be pictured as the area of a vertical curtain over that curve. Taking $f=1$ gives length; a nonnegative linear density gives the mass of a wire.
conditions: Use a regular $C^1$ parametrization on a compact interval: its velocity is continuous and nonzero in the interior, and it traces the curve once, with coincident endpoints allowed for a closed curve. A continuous scalar field on a rectifiable curve has a scalar line integral. Piecewise smooth extensions can be handled by additivity.
proof: A small parameter step gives displacement $r(t+\Delta t)-r(t)=r^{\prime}(t)\Delta t+o(\Delta t)$, so its length is approximately $\|r^{\prime}(t)\|\Delta t$. Substituting this into the scalar line Riemann sums gives the formula. Under a regular reparametrization, the speed factor and the substitution in $dt$ cancel; reversing direction leaves $ds$ unchanged.
example: The scene uses the unit circle $r(t)=(\cos t,\sin t,0)$ and scalar height $f=2+x$. Since $\|r^{\prime}(t)\|=1$, the curtain area is $\int_0^{2\pi}(2+\cos t)\,dt=4\pi$. The underlying circle length is $2\pi$.
pitfall: $ds$ is arc length along the base curve, not area under an arbitrary graph in the $t$-plane. Omitting the speed factor makes the answer depend incorrectly on the chosen parametrization.
task: Follow the curtain around one full revolution. Identify its largest and smallest heights, then explain why reversing traversal leaves its area unchanged.
insight: Scalar line integration measures along the geometry of a curve rather than along the clock used to traverse it.

title: Vector fields assign a direction at every point
subtitle: An arrow field becomes meaningful when compared with a path tangent.
definition: A vector field assigns a vector to each point in its domain, with the same input and output dimension. Its components are scalar functions. A plane vector field has two components; a space vector field has three. A $C^1$ field has continuous first partial derivatives on its open domain.
conditions: To integrate along a path, the entire path must lie in the field’s domain. Continuity along a compact smooth path suffices for its line integral. Arrows in the scene are samples of a continuously defined field; their finite density does not define the mathematics.
proof: For the scene’s field, $F(x,y,0)\cdot(x,y,0)=0$, so every nonzero field vector is perpendicular to the radius in the plane. On a circle, that is the tangent direction. Its norm is $\sqrt{x^2+y^2}$, so field strength increases with distance from the axis.
example: Along the unit circle $r(t)=(\cos t,\sin t,0)$, $F(r(t))=(-\sin t,\cos t,0)=r^{\prime}(t)$. The field therefore agrees exactly with the counterclockwise unit tangent. At $(1,0,0)$ it points toward positive $y$.
pitfall: The arrows specify the field, not a parametrized trajectory by themselves. In particular, a particle’s motion requires an additional differential equation or a chosen path; it need not follow the arrows.
task: At four points a quarter-turn apart, determine the vector from the formula and compare it with the circle’s counterclockwise tangent.
insight: Dot products with tangent vectors select the component of a field that contributes along a chosen motion.

title: Work and orientation along a curve
subtitle: Only the component along the displacement contributes.
formula: \begin{gathered}\int_C F\cdot dr=\int_a^b F(r(t))\cdot r^{\prime}(t)\,dt\\\int_{-C}F\cdot dr=-\int_CF\cdot dr\end{gathered}
definition: A vector line integral sums $F\cdot\Delta r$ along an oriented curve. It measures the accumulated tangential component of the field and, for a force field, the work done along the path. Unlike a scalar integral with $ds$, it retains the direction of displacement.
conditions: Assume $F$ is continuous on the path and choose a regular $C^1$ parametrization that traces the curve once in the stated orientation. Parametrizations with the same orientation give the same integral. Reversal changes its sign; tracing a loop repeatedly changes the traversal and counts it repeatedly.
proof: Replace each displacement in the vector Riemann sum by $r^{\prime}(t)\Delta t$ and pass to the limit to obtain the formula. For the reversed parametrization $s(t)=r(a+b-t)$, differentiation gives $s^{\prime}(t)=-r^{\prime}(a+b-t)$. A single-variable substitution then yields the negative original integral.
example: For the displayed counterclockwise unit circle and $F=(-y,x,0)$, the integrand is $F(r(t))\cdot r^{\prime}(t)=1$. Thus the full-circle integral is $2\pi$. A clockwise traversal gives $-2\pi$, even though the geometric curve and its length are unchanged.
pitfall: Replacing the dot product by $\|F\|\,\|r^{\prime}\|$ discards the angle and produces the wrong answer unless the vectors agree in direction everywhere. A closed path need not have zero integral; this example already gives a nonzero value.
task: Follow the circle in the field’s direction, then imagine reversing traversal. Explain the sign change locally at each point through the tangent dot product.
insight: Orientation carries essential information: the same curve can represent different signed accumulations.

title: Three differentials, one path
subtitle: Understand what $dx$, $dy$ and $dz$ actually measure.
definition: The coordinate integral $\int_C f\,dx$ sums $f$ times signed displacement in the $x$ coordinate. For $\mathbf r=(X,Y,Z)$, it is $\int_a^b f(\mathbf r(t))X^{\prime}(t)\,dt$; replace $X^{\prime}$ by $Y^{\prime}$ or $Z^{\prime}$ for $dy$ or $dz$. In these lectures, “first, second and third kinds” specifically refer to $dx,dy,dz$. Their sum with components $P,Q,R$ equals the vector line integral.
conditions: Let $\mathbf F=(P,Q,R)$ be continuous on an open set containing a piecewise $C^1$ curve. Use a parametrization traversing each piece once in the stated orientation. The same definitions apply in the plane by omitting $z$.
proof: On a short parameter interval, $\Delta x\approx X^{\prime}(t)\Delta t$. Substitution in the defining Riemann sum gives the coordinate formula. Adding the three component formulas gives $PX^{\prime}+QY^{\prime}+RZ^{\prime}=\mathbf F\cdot\mathbf r^{\prime}$. This also shows that reversing traversal negates all coordinate and vector line integrals.
example: The scene uses $\mathbf r(t)=(\cos t,\sin t,0)$ and $\mathbf F=(-y,x,0)$. Thus $-y\,dx=\sin^2t\,dt$ and $x\,dy=\cos^2t\,dt$. Each contributes $\pi$ on $0\le t\le2\pi$, giving total circulation $2\pi$.
pitfall: $ds=\|\mathbf r^{\prime}(t)\|dt$ is an unsigned length element. It is different from each of $dx,dy,dz$. For example $\int_C1\,ds=2\pi$ on a unit circle, whereas $\oint_C1\,dx=0$.
task: Trace one quarter of the circle and identify where $dx$ or $dy$ changes sign. Explain why $-y\,dx+x\,dy$ remains positive for counterclockwise travel.
insight: The arrows show local direction; the dot product determines the signed contribution. The integral formula, rather than the appearance of the arrows, establishes its value.

title: Assemble a path from pieces
subtitle: Corners change the parametrization, not the integral rule.
formula: \begin{gathered}\int_{C_1*\cdots*C_k}\mathbf F\cdot d\mathbf r=\sum_{j=1}^{k}\int_{C_j}\mathbf F\cdot d\mathbf r\\\mathbf r_{AB}(t)=A+t(B-A)\end{gathered}
definition: A piecewise-smooth oriented curve is a finite sequence of smooth arcs joined end to end. Integrate separately on each arc and add in traversal order. A directed segment from $A$ to $B$ has the affine parametrization $A+t(B-A)$, $0\le t\le1$. For scalar length integrals, the same additivity holds with $f\,ds$.
conditions: The field must be continuous along all pieces; each piece must have finite length. Corners and finitely many junction points are allowed. The subcurves must inherit the direction in which the full path is traversed.
proof: Split the parameter interval at its finitely many junctions and apply ordinary one-variable integral additivity. Each piece has its own velocity vector, so no derivative at the corner itself is needed. A finite collection of parameter points contributes no integral.
example: In the displayed field $\mathbf F=(2x,2y,2z)$, the curved path $\mathbf r(t)=(t,t^2,0)$ gives $\int_0^1(2t+4t^3)dt=2$. As a separate comparison, the broken path $(0,0,0)\to(1,0,0)\to(1,1,0)$ gives contributions $1+1=2$.
pitfall: Additivity applies to any integrable field, but equality of the curved and broken path integrals here is a special consequence of conservativeness. It is false for a general field.
task: Split the displayed parabola at $t=1/2$. Compute the first contribution $5/16$ and the second $27/16$, then verify that they sum to $2$.
insight: Changing from one arc to several is bookkeeping. Replacing the geometric path itself requires an additional reason such as a potential function.

title: Work is tangential accumulation
subtitle: Only the component along motion contributes.
formula: W=\int_C\mathbf F\cdot d\mathbf r=\int_C(\mathbf F\cdot\mathbf T)\,ds
definition: Work done by a force field is its vector line integral along the oriented trajectory. At a regular point, $\mathbf T=\mathbf r^{\prime}/\|\mathbf r^{\prime}\|$ is the oriented unit tangent. The scalar $\mathbf F\cdot\mathbf T$ is the force component along motion. Work along a closed curve is often called circulation.
conditions: Assume the field is continuous along a piecewise $C^1$ trajectory. The trajectory must avoid every point where the field is undefined. For example the point-mass gravitational field $-GMm\mathbf r/\|\mathbf r\|^3$ is not defined at the origin.
proof: Constant force on a short straight displacement does work $\mathbf F\cdot\Delta\mathbf r$. Summing over short segments and taking the Riemann-sum limit gives the line integral. Since $d\mathbf r=\mathbf T\,ds$, the normal component has zero dot product with displacement.
example: On the unit circle, $\mathbf F=(-y,x,0)$ is exactly the unit tangent for counterclockwise travel. The accumulated work from angle $0$ to $\theta$ is $\theta$; one full turn gives $2\pi$. Clockwise travel gives $-2\pi$.
pitfall: A field can do nonzero work around a closed loop. Returning to the starting point only forces zero work when the field is conservative. The formula $\mathbf F\cdot(B-A)$ assumes constant force.
task: Compare the force arrow with the tangent throughout one turn. Predict the sign when traversal is reversed before performing the integral.
insight: Direction and orientation are essential. A surface plot of field magnitude alone cannot determine work.

title: A potential remembers only endpoints
subtitle: The chain rule turns a path integral into a difference.
definition: A potential for a vector field $\mathbf F$ is a scalar function $\phi$ with $\mathbf F=\nabla\phi$. The Fundamental Theorem of Line Integrals says that integrating this gradient from $A$ to $B$ gives precisely the change in potential. A field admitting a potential is called conservative.
conditions: Let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open, $\phi\in C^1(U)$, and $C$ a piecewise $C^1$ oriented path in $U$ from $A$ to $B$. Neither convexity nor simple connectedness is needed once a potential on all of $U$ is already given.
proof: On each smooth piece the chain rule gives $(\phi\circ\mathbf r)^{\prime}(t)=\nabla\phi(\mathbf r(t))\cdot\mathbf r^{\prime}(t)$. The ordinary Fundamental Theorem of Calculus gives the endpoint difference on that piece. Summing telescopes all intermediate endpoints.
example: Here $\phi=x^2+y^2+z^2$ and $\mathbf F=(2x,2y,2z)$. Along the displayed parabola, work up to $\mathbf r(t)=(t,t^2,0)$ is $t^2+t^4$. Its final value is $\phi(1,1,0)-\phi(0,0,0)=2$.
pitfall: A “potential” is defined by its gradient in this course. In mechanics the potential energy $V$ often satisfies $\mathbf F=-\nabla V$ instead; then work is $V(A)-V(B)$. Also, do not silently reverse the path endpoints.
task: At $t=1/2$, compare the accumulated work $5/16$ with the potential at the moving point. Explain why the route from the origin cannot alter that value.
insight: The visual agreement is an illustration. Path independence follows for every admissible path from the chain-rule proof.

title: When does zero curl suffice?
subtitle: The domain is part of the theorem.
formula: \begin{gathered}\nabla\times F=0\iff F=\nabla\phi\\F\in C^1(U)\\U\text{ open and simply connected}\end{gathered}
definition: On an open path-connected domain, a continuous field is conservative exactly when integrals are path independent, equivalently when every closed piecewise-smooth path has integral zero. For a $C^1$ plane field $(P,Q)$, the local test is $Q_x=P_y$. In three dimensions the three corresponding equations are summarized by $\nabla\times\mathbf F=0$.
conditions: The zero-curl test is sufficient on an open simply connected domain: it is path connected and every closed loop can be continuously contracted to a point within the domain. This loop condition is more precise than “no holes,” especially in three dimensions. Conservativeness itself does not require simple connectedness.
proof: If $\mathbf F=\nabla\phi$ and $\mathbf F\in C^1$, then $\phi\in C^2$ and equality of mixed partials gives zero curl. Conversely, zero curl gives local potentials; on a simply connected domain these combine consistently into a global potential. Equivalently, define $\phi(p)$ by integrating from a base point; vanishing loop integrals make this definition independent of path.
example: The displayed field $2(x,y,z)$ has the global potential $x^2+y^2+z^2$. For a contrasting exact example, $\mathbf G=(-y/(x^2+y^2),x/(x^2+y^2))$ has zero plane curl on $\mathbb R^2\setminus\{0\}$ but circulation $2\pi$ around the unit circle, so it is not conservative there.
pitfall: You may not apply Green’s Theorem across the missing origin in the contrasting example. To construct a potential by integrating $P$ in $x$, the integration “constant” may be a function of the remaining coordinates.
task: Explain which hypothesis fails for the punctured-plane example. Then find a potential for $(2xy,1+x^2-y^2)$ by starting with $\phi=x^2y+h(y)$.
insight: The answer is $\phi=x^2y+y-y^3/3+C$. The topology governs whether locally compatible derivatives produce one globally defined function.

title: Green’s Theorem
subtitle: Add tiny circulations; interior edges cancel.
definition: Green’s Theorem equates circulation along the boundary of a plane region with the integral of its scalar curl inside. A simple closed curve has a bounded interior and an unbounded exterior by the Jordan curve theorem. Positive boundary orientation means the region remains on the left as one travels.
conditions: For the standard course case, let $D$ be the closure of a bounded region with a piecewise $C^1$ simple closed boundary. Let $P,Q\in C^1(U)$ on an open neighborhood $U$ of the whole closed region. For a region with holes, include every boundary component: outer boundaries counterclockwise and hole boundaries clockwise.
proof: For a rectangle, integrate $Q_x$ and $-P_y$ by the ordinary Fundamental Theorem of Calculus to obtain its four oriented edge integrals. Adding adjacent rectangles cancels integrals on shared edges. A limiting subdivision argument gives the result for admissible regions; the animation depicts this cancellation, not a substitute for that argument.
example: The scene uses $\mathbf F=(-y/2,x/2,0)$ and the unit disk. Its plane curl is $1$. On the unit-circle boundary, $\mathbf F\cdot\mathbf r^{\prime}=1/2$, so both the boundary integral and the area integral equal $\pi$.
pitfall: Checking smoothness only on the boundary is insufficient: the field must be defined and $C^1$ throughout a neighborhood of the region. The symbol $\oint$ means a closed path; its sign still depends on the stated orientation.
task: Follow the positive boundary direction. Explain why reversing it gives $-\pi$ while the unsigned area of the disk stays $\pi$.
insight: The scalar curl records circulation per small oriented area. Green’s Theorem accumulates those local contributions over the interior.

title: Measure area from the boundary
subtitle: A line integral can recover an interior quantity.
definition: Choose a plane field whose scalar curl is identically $1$. Green’s Theorem then turns its circulation into the area of the enclosed region. Three convenient choices are $(0,x)$, $(-y,0)$ and $(-y/2,x/2)$. The last treats the two coordinates symmetrically.
conditions: The boundary must be a positively oriented piecewise-smooth simple closed curve, or all consistently oriented boundary components of an admissible bounded region. A curve that crosses itself generally yields a signed area with multiplicities instead of the ordinary area of one simple interior.
proof: For each listed field, $Q_x-P_y=1$. Substitute directly into Green’s Theorem to get $\iint_D1\,dA$. The three boundary expressions agree because their differences integrate exact differentials around a closed curve.
example: The unit-circle scene gives $\frac12\int_0^{2\pi}(\cos^2t+\sin^2t)dt=\pi$. For the lecture’s ellipse, use $(x,y)=(a\cos t,b\sin t)$ with $a,b>0$. Then $x\,dy-y\,dx=ab\,dt$, and the area is $\pi ab$.
pitfall: The formula gives a negative number for clockwise traversal. That negative value is signed area, not a negative geometric area. The planimeter application relies on this distinction.
task: Compute the ellipse result without integrating its upper and lower graph functions. Identify exactly where the product $ab$ enters.
insight: An appropriate differential expression packages the interior area into the motion of a point around its boundary.

title: A surface is a two-parameter image
subtitle: Separate the parameter domain from the surface.
formula: \begin{gathered}r(u,v)=\begin{pmatrix}2\sin u\cos v\\2\sin u\sin v\\2\cos u\end{pmatrix}\\0\le u\le\pi,\quad0\le v\le2\pi\end{gathered}
definition: A surface parametrization maps a two-dimensional parameter region into $\mathbb R^3$. In the course definition, the region has nonempty connected interior, the map is continuous on the region, and its restriction to the interior is a homeomorphism onto its image. Thus interior parameter points give unique surface points with a continuous inverse. Boundary identifications may still occur.
conditions: For the sphere chart shown, $u$ is the polar angle from the positive $z$ axis and $v$ is the azimuth. Its interior map is one-to-one away from the seam and poles. A geometric surface point is an interior point if some valid chart puts it in the image of a parameter interior; this does not depend on one chosen chart.
proof: The displayed coordinates satisfy $x^2+y^2+z^2=4$. Conversely, every point of the radius-$2$ sphere has such spherical coordinates. Fixing $u$ produces a latitude circle; fixing $v$ produces a meridian. Away from poles and seam the inverse is locally continuous.
example: A cylindrical example from the lecture is $\mathbf r(u,v)=(2\cos u,v,2\sin u)$, describing $x^2+z^2=4$ with axis along $y$. Restricting the parameter region selects a patch rather than changing the parametrization formula.
pitfall: A seam in a rectangular parameter domain need not be an edge of the geometric surface. The sphere has no edge. Likewise, a pole at which spherical coordinates degenerate is not a singular point of the sphere.
task: Vary $u$ along the meridian $v=0.7$. Identify the latitude through the selected point and explain what varying $v$ would trace.
insight: Parameter coordinates label points; their numerical spacing does not measure physical distance or area on the surface.

title: Two tangents determine a normal
subtitle: Regularity is the rank-two condition.
formula: \begin{gathered}\mathbf n=\frac{\mathbf r_u\times\mathbf r_v}{\|\mathbf r_u\times\mathbf r_v\|}\\\mathbf r_u\times\mathbf r_v\ne0\end{gathered}
definition: Holding one parameter fixed and varying the other produces two curves on the surface. Their velocities are $\mathbf r_u$ and $\mathbf r_v$. A smooth regular parametrization has continuous first partial derivatives and nonzero cross product at every interior parameter point. The differential then has rank two, and these velocities span the tangent plane.
conditions: The displayed normal formula applies wherever the chart is regular. Smoothness of a surface at a point means that at least one regular chart covers that point. Piecewise-smooth surfaces are finite unions of smooth patches meeting only along their edges.
proof: The cross product is perpendicular to both parameter velocities. Nonvanishing makes them linearly independent, so their span is a two-dimensional tangent plane. Dividing the cross product by its length gives one unit normal; its negative is the only other unit normal.
example: For the radius-$2$ sphere, $\|\mathbf r_u\|=2$, $\|\mathbf r_v\|=2\sin u$, and the tangents are orthogonal. Hence $\mathbf r_u\times\mathbf r_v=4\sin u\,\mathbf n$, where $\mathbf n=\mathbf r/2$ points outward for $0<u<\pi$.
pitfall: The vanishing cross product at $u=0$ or $u=\pi$ is a failure of this chart. A local graph over an appropriate coordinate plane supplies a regular chart at either pole. A cone tip, by contrast, has no tangent plane of this kind.
task: As the moving point approaches a pole, inspect which parameter tangent shrinks. Explain why its shrinking does not flatten or puncture the sphere.
insight: Regularity concerns the local geometry represented by a chart. Distinguishing a coordinate failure from a geometric singularity prevents incorrect conclusions.

title: A tiny rectangle becomes a parallelogram
subtitle: The cross product measures area distortion.
definition: A small parameter rectangle with side lengths $\Delta u,\Delta v$ maps, to first order, to a tangent parallelogram with edge vectors $\mathbf r_u\Delta u$ and $\mathbf r_v\Delta v$. Its area is $\|\mathbf r_u\times\mathbf r_v\|\Delta u\Delta v$. This factor converts parameter area into surface area.
conditions: Use a regular $C^1$ chart that covers the surface once apart from boundary identifications. The course’s “nice” assumption additionally requires a bounded parameter region with boundary of zero area and bounded parameter derivatives. Finite collections of such patches may be added along edges.
proof: The cross-product magnitude is the product of the two edge lengths times the sine of their angle. Approximate the surface by tangent parallelograms and refine the subdivision. Regularity and the stated boundedness permit the Riemann sums to converge to the displayed area integral.
example: For the radius-$2$ sphere, $dS=4\sin u\,du\,dv$. The whole area is $\int_0^{2\pi}\int_0^\pi4\sin u\,du\,dv=16\pi$. The cap $0\le u\le\alpha$ has area $8\pi(1-\cos\alpha)$.
pitfall: Using $du\,dv$ alone incorrectly treats the parameter grid as physically uniform. Near a sphere’s pole, equal increments of azimuth cover much less area than they do near its equator.
task: Compare equal parameter cells near the equator and near a pole. Use $4\sin u$ to predict their relative areas.
insight: The geometric distortion is exactly quantified by the differential; the mesh suggests the pattern, while the cross product gives the exact factor.

title: Integrate a density over a surface
subtitle: Value times actual area, with no orientation sign.
definition: A scalar surface integral accumulates a scalar density over actual surface area. If $f$ is a nonnegative surface mass density, the result is mass. Choosing $f=1$ gives surface area. For a surface made from finitely many patches meeting only along edges, add the integrals of all patches.
conditions: The course definition assumes a nice regular surface parametrization and a continuous scalar field bounded on the surface. The value is independent of admissible reparametrization. A surface covered several times by a parametrization is generally counted with that multiplicity.
proof: Multiply each approximate tangent-parallelogram area by the sampled density and take the Riemann-sum limit. Under a change of parameters, the surface cross-product factor gains the absolute value of the parameter Jacobian, exactly canceled by the change-of-variables formula. Thus the integral depends on the surface, not its coordinate labels.
example: On the displayed sphere, $f=z^2=4\cos^2u$ gives $\iint_S z^2\,dS=\int_0^{2\pi}\int_0^\pi16\cos^2u\sin u\,du\,dv=64\pi/3$. For a graph $z=g(x,y)$, the area factor is $\sqrt{1+g_x^2+g_y^2}$.
pitfall: A scalar integral $\iint_Sf\,dS$ is unchanged when the orientation is reversed. This is different from flux. The graph formula may have unbounded derivatives at a chart edge, so check its hypotheses or use another chart.
task: As a separate graph example, derive the lecture’s area of $z=x^2+y^2$ below $z=9$: $2\pi\int_0^3r\sqrt{1+4r^2}\,dr=\frac\pi6(37^{3/2}-1)$.
insight: A surface integral combines two independent ingredients: the density at the point and the area distortion of the parametrization.

title: Choose a continuous side
subtitle: A normal at one point is local; orientation is global.
definition: An orientable smooth surface admits a continuous unit normal field over its whole surface interior. Choosing such a field is an orientation. A connected orientable surface has two choices, $\mathbf n$ and $-\mathbf n$. Graph surfaces have the natural upward choice with positive third component. Boundaries of solids have the natural outward choice.
conditions: A parametrization supplies a local normal via $\mathbf r_u\times\mathbf r_v$. On overlaps, local normal choices must agree to give one global orientation. For a boundary of a solid, “outward” means pointing away from the solid, including into any cavity.
proof: At a regular point the normal line has exactly two unit vectors. Continuity prohibits switching between them arbitrarily along a connected patch. On a sphere, $\mathbf r/2$ is a global continuous outward normal. On a Möbius strip, transporting a local normal around its central loop returns its negative, preventing a globally consistent choice.
example: The sphere scene shows outward normals. In the graph $z=1-x^2-y^2$, the upward area vector is $(2x,2y,1)\,dx\,dy$. A standard Möbius parametrization is $((1+v\cos(u/2))\cos u,(1+v\cos(u/2))\sin u,v\sin(u/2))$, with $0\le u\le2\pi$ and a sufficiently small width $|v|\le a<1$.
pitfall: Every regular surface point has two local normal choices; this does not imply global orientability. The sphere illustrates an orientable case. The Möbius obstruction requires following a normal around its identified seam and is not demonstrated by the sphere itself.
task: At a point on the lower hemisphere, compare “outward” with “upward.” Explain why outward on a closed sphere cannot mean positive $z$ component everywhere.
insight: Orientation specifies which sign the flux uses. Scalar surface area is meaningful even on a nonorientable surface.
